I thought Muck was just another goofy survival game that people played for laughs.

I was wrong.

The graphics are simple. The gameplay is simple. The goal is basically to survive, gather resources, build stuff, and try not to get absolutely destroyed by whatever decides to spawn next.

And somehow, it works.

There's something ridiculously satisfying about starting with nothing, punching trees, finding better gear, and slowly turning yourself into an overpowered monster. Then nighttime comes around and you realize you may have made a terrible mistake.

The enemies are chaotic, the combat is surprisingly fun, and the whole game has this weird combination of panic and comedy that kept me playing far longer than I expected.

What I love most is how easy it is to just jump into Muck. You don't need to understand some massive story or memorize a hundred systems. You just start playing, make questionable decisions, get stronger, die horribly, and immediately think, "Okay, one more run."

I've played survival games with better graphics, bigger maps, and way more content.

I don't remember most of them.

I'll remember Muck.

Some games are designed to be impressive.

Muck is designed to make you laugh, suffer, and somehow have a great time doing both.

100% recommended.

Muck: Humanity's Greatest Mistake

There are moments in history that define the rise and fall of civilization. The invention of fire. The wheel. The moon landing. And then, in a moment that can only be described as the universe's cruelest practical joke, Muck entered existence. At that instant, the collective progress of humanity stopped, looked directly at this digital monstrosity, and quietly asked, "Why?"

Muck is not a game. Calling it a game is an insult to games. Chess is a game. Soccer is a game. Hide-and-seek is a game. Muck is a sentient psychological weapon disguised as downloadable software. It doesn't entertain you. It studies you. It identifies your remaining fragments of happiness and systematically obliterates them with the enthusiasm of a supernova.

The moment you click "Play," your computer doesn't launch a game—it opens a portal to a dimension where common sense has been outlawed. You spawn with a rock, no explanation, and approximately thirty-seven seconds before the local ecosystem collectively decides that your continued existence is unacceptable. Every tree stands there mocking you. Every chest is bait. Every creature wakes up each morning with one singular goal: ruining your day in increasingly creative ways.

The combat system feels like it was engineered by an ancient council whose only qualification was "professional hater." You swing your weapon with the confidence of a seasoned warrior, only to discover that the enemy has somehow bent the laws of physics, ignored your attack entirely, and launched you so far into the atmosphere that commercial airlines begin asking if you'd like a window seat.

Every single enemy in Muck behaves as though you personally offended their ancestors. Goblins? They hate you. Golems? They hate you. Dragons? They hate you. Chickens? Somehow they probably hate you too. If a blade of grass could attack, it absolutely would.

Nighttime is not "hard." Nighttime is the digital recreation of the apocalypse. The sun disappears for half a second before every nightmare ever conceived simultaneously clocks in for their shift. The island becomes less of a survival game and more of a mandatory participation event in your own downfall. The soundtrack doesn't comfort you—it sounds like it's celebrating your inevitable demise.

The loot system deserves its own category of crimes against humanity. Every chest exists solely to convince you that maybe—just maybe—this time you'll get something useful. Instead, you receive the gaming equivalent of a participation trophy moments before a creature the size of a shopping mall deletes your entire health bar with one mildly annoyed swing.

And the bosses...

The bosses aren't difficult because they're well designed. They're difficult because they apparently negotiated exclusive rights to every law of the universe. They move faster than logic, hit harder than continental drift, and possess enough health to survive the heat death of the cosmos. Fighting one feels less like battling a monster and more like filing paperwork against an asteroid.

Multiplayer somehow elevates this disaster into an entirely new genre of suffering. Your friends transform from trusted allies into opportunistic goblins who will accidentally awaken ancient horrors, steal every valuable item, disappear during every boss fight, and then ask, "Bro, why did you die?" while standing safely on the opposite side of the map.

The optimization is your least concern, because by this point your graphics card has already accepted its fate. Even your PC begins questioning your life choices. Somewhere deep inside the cooling fans, a tiny voice whispers, "We were built for better than this."

If an alien civilization discovered Muck floating through space, they wouldn't invade Earth. They would assume the planet had already fallen.

The emotional damage inflicted by this game cannot be measured by science. Therapists would require therapists after hearing a complete description of a single play session. Philosophers would spend centuries debating whether Muck was created as entertainment or as a cautionary tale about unchecked ambition. Historians would erase it from textbooks out of mercy.

To recommend Muck to another human being is to betray the very concept of friendship. It is the social equivalent of replacing someone's parachute with a backpack full of bricks and saying, "You'll figure it out." It is the digital version of inviting someone to a birthday party only to reveal it is actually an active volcano.

If every copy of Muck were gathered together, launched into the center of the Sun, and then the Sun itself was fired into a black hole that was subsequently erased from existence, one could argue that the universe had only just begun repairing the damage.

In conclusion, Muck is, in this wildly exaggerated and entirely satirical essay, not merely a bad game—it is a reality-distorting anomaly, a cosmic paperwork error, an offense against joy itself, and the closest humanity has come to accidentally downloading an eldritch curse. It should not be recommended to friends, family, coworkers, strangers, historians, archaeologists, extraterrestrials, future civilizations, parallel universes, or any living organism capable of experiencing disappointment.

Should anyone ask whether they should play Muck, the only responsible response—according to this intentionally over-the-top rant—is to gaze solemnly toward the horizon, remember the fallen, and simply whisper:

"No. Save yourself."

HOW TO BEAT THE GAME!

Beating the game is fairly simple, albeit pretty luck based. Get a rock, mine 1 tree and immediately try to find a village. If you do find one, loot the entire village (EXCEPT FOR THE CHIEF'S CHEST!) and search for the villager with a tree on it's head or the one with the helmet. Try to get Adamantite or Mithril equipments from them. If you're lucky enough, you might get an obamium sword. Mine gold ores as well, very very useful to get a crap ton of money at the start of the game by smelting them into gold bars and turning them into coins using the anvil.

For food, just get a crap ton of apple, or the red and yellow mushrooms. Those are the only sources of food you need to survive, other foods are only if you're feeling fancy.

 Keep mining upwards based on your equipments (For example, if you have a Mithril pickaxe, mine Adamantites and then Obamium.) After you get a crap ton of gold, get the smaller, wooden chests first and try to obtain either +ATK speed, health regeneration or +Movement speed. Then go for the blue chests, and try to get the most important powerups in the game which are Crimson Dagger, Knut's Hammer, Horseshoe, Sniper Scope, and Dracula. Those will carry you throughout the end game. You need to get at least a full set Mithril or Adamantite armors and weapons before the first boss spawns based on your difficulty (Day 6 for Easy, day 4 for Normal and idk about the Gamer difficulty because I didn't bother trying it.) And then you're all set.

Overall, very fun and simple.

Muck is a survival roguelike that began as a joke project but unexpectedly turned into one of the more entertaining and addictive multiplayer survival games on Steam. Created by YouTuber Dani, the game initially appears chaotic and simplistic, almost as if it was never meant to be taken seriously. However, beneath its meme-inspired presentation is a surprisingly effective blend of crafting, exploration, combat, and roguelike progression that creates a fast-paced survival experience full of unpredictable moments and constant escalation. What starts as a simple resource-gathering adventure quickly transforms into a frantic fight for survival against increasingly dangerous enemies and massive bosses.

The core gameplay loop revolves around surviving on a randomly generated island by gathering materials, crafting tools, and preparing for increasingly difficult nights. During the daytime, players cut trees, mine rocks, collect food, and search for resources needed to create stronger equipment. At night, the game changes dramatically as hostile enemies begin spawning in large numbers, forcing players to defend themselves while trying to continue progressing. This constant cycle of preparation and chaos gives the game a strong sense of momentum because there is always pressure to become stronger before the next wave of enemies arrives.

One of the game’s biggest strengths is its pacing. Unlike many survival games that spend hours focused on realism and slow progression, Muck moves at an extremely aggressive speed. Resources are collected quickly, upgrades appear constantly, and combat escalates almost immediately. Players can go from using primitive wooden tools to wielding powerful weapons and fighting giant monsters within a relatively short amount of time. The game avoids unnecessary downtime and instead focuses on keeping players engaged through nonstop progression and increasingly dangerous encounters.

Combat is simple but surprisingly satisfying because of how chaotic battles become later in a run. Players fight enemies using swords, bows, shields, and various upgraded weapons while dodging attacks and managing stamina. The mechanics themselves are not especially deep, but the speed and intensity of encounters make every fight exciting. Enemy numbers increase rapidly, bosses become more aggressive, and surviving later nights often feels like barely controlled chaos. The frantic nature of combat becomes one of the game’s most entertaining qualities, especially once powerful enemies begin appearing alongside massive waves of smaller creatures.

The roguelike elements add another layer of addictiveness to the experience. Throughout each session, players open treasure chests containing passive upgrades that dramatically improve their abilities. These bonuses can increase movement speed, health regeneration, attack damage, stamina, mining efficiency, and many other attributes. Because upgrades stack continuously during a run, characters gradually become absurdly powerful by the late game. This creates a satisfying progression curve where players constantly feel stronger while enemies simultaneously become more threatening.

Multiplayer is where Muck becomes truly memorable. Playing with friends transforms the game into a hilarious and unpredictable survival experience filled with panic, teamwork, and accidental disasters. Communication becomes essential during nighttime attacks and boss encounters, especially when multiple enemies overwhelm the group simultaneously. The game’s chaotic systems naturally create funny moments, whether it is a friend accidentally summoning a powerful boss too early or an entire team being chased across the map during a disastrous night fight. The unpredictability of multiplayer sessions gives the game enormous replay value.

Another reason the game works so well is its accessibility. The crafting systems are easy to understand, the controls are straightforward, and the mechanics are simple enough for almost anyone to pick up quickly. Muck avoids overwhelming players with complicated survival systems or excessive realism. Instead, it focuses entirely on action, exploration, and progression. This approachable design makes it easy for new players to jump into the chaos without spending hours learning complicated mechanics.

Visually, the game uses a low-poly art style that fits its goofy personality perfectly. The graphics are intentionally simple, with colorful environments and exaggerated enemy designs that keep the gameplay easy to read during hectic battles. While the visuals are not technically impressive, the clean art direction works well because it prioritizes clarity and performance over realism. The simplistic presentation also reinforces the comedic tone that defines much of the experience.

The soundtrack and audio design help maintain the game’s energetic atmosphere. Calm exploration music contrasts nicely with the intense combat themes that play during enemy attacks and boss fights. Sound effects are loud and exaggerated, matching the game’s chaotic identity. Combined with the rapid pacing, the audio helps every encounter feel exciting even when the mechanics themselves remain relatively simple.

Despite its strengths, Muck is far from a perfectly polished game. Balance issues are common, and certain enemy combinations or unlucky item spawns can make some runs feel unfairly difficult. The randomness that creates excitement can also occasionally lead to frustrating situations where players are overwhelmed before they have enough resources to defend themselves properly. New players may struggle during the early hours because the game offers little guidance beyond basic survival mechanics.

The lack of permanent progression may also disappoint some players. Since most upgrades disappear after each run, long-term advancement relies almost entirely on player skill and experience rather than unlock systems. While this structure fits the roguelike design, some players may eventually feel that the game lacks larger long-term goals outside surviving longer and experimenting with different strategies.

Technical roughness is another noticeable aspect of the experience. Bugs, strange physics interactions, and occasional glitches appear regularly, though many players treat these imperfections as part of the game’s charm rather than serious flaws. The game’s chaotic nature often turns even technical issues into funny multiplayer moments instead of completely ruining the experience.

What ultimately makes Muck so enjoyable is how confidently it embraces its absurdity while still delivering genuinely fun gameplay underneath the memes and chaos. The game understands that its greatest strength is unpredictability. Every run feels different, every multiplayer session creates new ridiculous situations, and the constant escalation keeps players engaged even when things become completely out of control.

For fans of survival games, roguelikes, and chaotic multiplayer experiences, Muck offers an addictive and entertaining adventure filled with fast progression, frantic combat, and endless unpredictable moments. It may not be the most polished survival game available, but its energy, humor, and nonstop chaos make it one of the most memorable indie survival experiences on Steam.

Muck is what happens when you take survival crafting, remove all sanity, and then tell players “good luck, figure it out.”
You spawn in with nothing, immediately start punching trees like every survival game ever… and then the game responds by spawning increasingly angry creatures that strongly disagree with your life choices. The longer you survive, the less it feels like a peaceful crafting experience and more like you accidentally started a war with nature itself.
The gameplay loop is simple but dangerously addictive: gather resources during the day, build whatever you can before night hits, and then survive the nightly wave of enemies that scale from “mild inconvenience” to “why is that thing flying at me at Mach 3.”
What makes Muck funny is how fast it escalates. You’ll start confidently building a base, and ten minutes later you’re kiting monsters in circles with a wooden weapon while questioning why you thought this was a good idea solo.
Multiplayer turns it into organized chaos. Someone is always hoarding gold “for upgrades,” someone else is already dead, and at least one player is running away screaming while carrying something important they don’t understand how to use.
And then there’s the RNG—sometimes you get strong gear early and feel like a god, and sometimes you get a rock and emotional damage.
Overall, Muck is fast, chaotic, and way more stressful than it looks, but that’s exactly why it’s so fun. It’s survival crafting distilled into pure panic with occasional moments of victory before everything inevitably falls apart again.

Oh my holy meh. Overhyped to the moon and back. Tried to combine survival and roguelike game-feel and ended up with neither.

Overall, the game is built around fast paced roguelike elements, but progression is slow. Like a combination of Minecraft and a .io survivor game. Makes for a very slow and casual atmosphere, hijacked by the disturbingly fast paced combat every 3 minutes. 

No saving AT ALL is a sin of its own in a survival game. (Speculative if making a save system was even possible from the developer.) Combat mechanics are clunky and poorly refined, resource gathering is insanely tedious for how fast the game urges you to progress, and mandatory boss fights are unfairly punishing early on. The roguelike elements are cool and addicting, of course, but the survival aspect feels like a side objective despite being the only way to progress.

* If you want to play a survival game with interesting progression, strategy, and vibes, then stay far away. 
* If you want the adrenaline rush of a roguelike with high stakes, quick tactical thinking, and satisfying skill reward, then stay further away. 
* If you've ever wanted to spend an hour or two building up a base and cool upgrades/gear only to have it permanently deleted by "Gonk", then this is the game for you.

First, adding a mini-map directly on the HUD would be much better than having to press 'M' every time, which feels a bit clunky. Second, I’d suggest allowing players to press 'TAB' to exit NPC dialogues quickly. I’ve died way too many times because I couldn't back out fast enough when a boss spawned and one-shot me.

Overall, for a free-to-play game, it's a solid experience and I highly recommend it.

3. This game really doesn't need to be a roguelike. Especially when you can build and customize and things like that. It just makes it that much more infuriating when you die. It doesn't give you a feeling that you need to come back like other roguelikes. It's just a weird thing to force onto players. 

4. The revive timer goes up every time I die. What is even the point of that?

5. The day/night cycle is just way too fast. You'll get excess enemies from the night time and it'll be night again before you can kill them all.

6. This isn't really a complaint I just want to know what the hell creative mode is. I thought I'd be able to revive from the dead or something but that didn't work.

There's a ton more complaints I would cover but those are just the things off of the top of my head.
Overall, it just feels like another game where all the difficulty just comes from weird annoying choices.

I booted this up expecting survival. What I got was a boot camp run by rocks.

Muck feels like it was designed to punish curiosity. You punch trees, get jumped by goblins with Olympic sprint speed, and die before you’ve finished asking “what does this item do?” The progression is chaos pretending to be depth. Crafting is buried under RNG, enemies scale like they’re on pre-workout, and the game explains almost nothing, then acts offended when you fail.

Combat is a mash-fest where timing barely matters and positioning matters even less. Half the time you’re not fighting enemies, you’re fighting the UI. Solo play is basically a speedrun to frustration. Co-op only works if your friends enjoy screaming and blaming each other for dying to a green dude with a stick.

Yes, it’s free. That explains a lot, but it doesn’t excuse the balance. This feels less like a survival game and more like a stress test for patience. If you enjoy dying repeatedly while wondering what you did wrong, congrats, you’ve found your home. If not, uninstalling is the most satisfying mechanic in the game.

Review of Muck

Muck is a fast-paced survival roguelike that blends resource gathering, crafting, and combat into short but intense play sessions. The core gameplay loop is simple: collect resources during the day, craft better gear, and prepare to survive increasingly difficult enemies that attack at night.

One thing I really liked about Muck is how accessible it is. The mechanics are easy to learn, but the game still offers a good level of challenge, especially as enemy difficulty ramps up quickly. The progression system with power-ups and items keeps each run feeling a bit different, and co-op multiplayer adds a lot of fun and chaos when playing with friends.

However, the game can feel repetitive after longer play sessions. The visuals are very simple, which fits the game’s style but may not appeal to everyone. Solo play can also become quite punishing, as the difficulty increases rapidly and leaves little room for mistakes.

Overall, I would recommend Muck, especially to players who enjoy survival games and roguelikes, or those looking for a fun co-op experience with friends. It may not offer deep long-term variety, but it provides plenty of entertainment in short bursts and is well worth trying.

Recommended (But Please Chill With the Difficulty Whiplash)

I do like this game. I really do. It’s a cool concept, it’s fun with friends, and for a free game it offers a surprisingly unique experience.

That said, the difficulty curve feels less like a curve and more like a sudden drop-off cliff.

For the first five days, everything is fine. You’re dealing with a couple goblins, some ankle-biters, maybe a golem if the game’s feeling spicy. You get into a rhythm. You’re surviving. You’re feeling confident. You think, “Yeah, I’ve got this.”

Then around day seven — always right when I’m about to smelt mithril — the game decides it’s time to ruin my life.

Suddenly there’s a full-on boss showing up. Guardian, Chief, or the mysterious “kills you before you can read the name” guy. I spend the entire day just barely defeating this thing, using every resource I have. Victory feels earned… until the next wave arrives before I’ve had any chance to recover.

From there it’s a slow, inevitable death spiral. No food. No time. No breathing room. I get starved out and wiped somewhere around day 10 or 11. Every. Single. Time.

I’ve tried building bigger bases, but that doesn’t help much when wood — seemingly the only construction material available (at least within my 4 hours of play) — might as well be cardboard against the absolute bullet-hell happening outside. Defenses don’t scale nearly as fast as the enemies do, and it shows.

Another thing that would massively improve the experience: saving. Longer runs start to feel pointless when you know that one bad wave means losing everything. After investing real time into a run, wiping and starting from scratch doesn’t feel challenging — it just feels discouraging.

All that said, I still recommend the game. It’s free, it’s different, and it’s genuinely fun to mess around in with friends. It just desperately needs some difficulty balancing and a way to respect the time players put into longer sessions.

Muck is a radiant paradox, a game that fuses simplicity with exhilaration in a way that feels almost mythic. Its world, though minimal, carries a peculiar and enchanting grandeur that invites you to savor every frantic strike of a tree, every desperate dash across the fields, and every triumphant moment of survival. Each day feels like an earnest stanza in a larger adventure, while each night becomes a wild symphony of danger, humor, and unwavering defiance.

The creatures that emerge from the dark may bring chaos, yet their presence elevates the experience into a poetic duel between courage and calamity. Even failure becomes part of the charm, a playful reminder that the journey itself holds the true reward.

In its cooperative heart, Muck achieves something rare. Laughter shared across the battlefield, last-second rescues, and victories forged through sheer insistence transform friends into folk heroes. This game captures the pure essence of joy and camaraderie, offering an experience that lingers long after the final sunrise.

Muck is not just a pastime. It is an ode to chaos, a celebration of imperfect brilliance, and a testament to the unexpected beauty hidden within even the most unpredictable adventures.

Eğer "hayatta kalma" oyunlarının en basit ve eğlenceli hali ne diye sorarsanız, Muck işte size en kötü örneği sunar. Oyunun grafiklerinden başlayalım; gerçekten 2000'lerin başı gibi bir his veriyor. 3D modellemeler, çevre tasarımları ve animasyonlar tamamen amatörce. İlk başta eğlenceli gibi gelebilir, ama hızla sıkıcı ve rahatsız edici hale geliyor.

Oynanış ise tam bir fiyasko! Her şey çok yüzeysel ve tekrarcı. Yalnızca ormanlarda koşarak kaynak topluyorsunuz, sonra bu kaynakları daha fazla kaynak toplamak için harcıyorsunuz. Yapacak bir şey bulamadığınızda sadece kötü yapay zekâya sahip yaratıklarla savaşıyorsunuz ki bu da çok keyifli değil.

Ve tabii ki çok "zorlu" olduğu iddia edilen düşmanlar, aslında sadece sayıca fazla ve zayıf yapay zekâya sahipler. Bazen düşmanlar aniden ortaya çıkıyor ve bir dakika sonra öldürülüyor. Yani tam anlamıyla "hayatta kalma" duygusu yaratmıyor.

Multiplayer'da ise oyun daha da berbat bir hâl alıyor. Bağlantı sorunları, sunucu hataları, lag ve takım arkadaşlarıyla iletişim kurmak zor... Bu oyunun çoğu zaman tek başına bile oynanması zor.

Sonuç olarak, Muck kesinlikle zaman kaybı. Eğer kaliteli bir hayatta kalma deneyimi arıyorsanız, Muck yerine çok daha iyi alternatifler mevcut. Tekrar oynamayı asla düşünmem ve bu parayı verdiğime pişmanım.

I won’t lie, the game looks like a turd.  You can call it “stylised” as much as you like, but the Graphics are very low effort.   

But Graphics don’t make a good game, right?  I mean Minecraft is brilliant. 

Unfortunately in my humble opinion this isn’t even a fun game to play.  It’s similar to Minecraft, but weirder, very frustrating and a lot harder.  

The game starts you off seemingly giving you a tutorial, but then ends after you craft your first workbench leaving you up S**t Creek without a paddle.  The game does not provide you with means to quickly craft or obtain any weapons and armour to help defend yourself from the too fast, difficult and relentless enemies that will gladly pursue you all the way across the world until either you or they are dead.  And when it goes dark, they spawn just to come right after you, so there’s no avoiding them.  Given this is a permadeath game, I think that is totally unacceptable. 

Given that crafting and building seem to be the made focus of this game the tutorial should have gone a little longer to teach you how to make, tools, weapons and armour and maybe where to get the ingredients from for tools.  Apparently you need bark to craft a tool, well I chopped a fair few trees down and got wood, but didn’t get any bark.  So where’s the bark??? 

You get hungry too quickly.  The cows do absolutely nothing when you attack them.   They just stand there in silence while you beat them to death with whatever you are carrying.

There are chests mysteriously lying all over the place and instead of simply opening them, breaking them open with something or unlocking them, as any normal person would expect, you need the right amount of coins in your inventory. Yes that’s right; you need “The right amount of coins in your inventory to open a chest.”   Which totally makes sense, right?  Yeah-Nah.

I like open world survival games like Minecraft, and although Muck is similar, I just can’t recommend it.   But for a very similar hidden gem, I can recommend “Fallen Angel: Hell Survival” over this for sure, especially if you don’t mind playing this genre as single player.  The graphics are nice and at least it’s fun to play.

Good game, hard at beginning but when u figure out u just need to fight and open chests it becomes easy.
So far these are tips i would give :
1. Armor is useless - game difficulty scales as time goes on so u have only time to build axe pick and a weapon.
2. Open as many chests as u can - more items = u become more OP to the point u can one shot no matter the weapon/tool ur holding
3. Fight as much as u can - those battle pillars that u can fight 3 enemies to get an item from completing do them early since it will spawn easy enemies to kill so u get gold for more chests and u get an item after killing them
4. Dont stay in one place keep moving - u will exhaust chests in ur area if u stay in one place and waste time going back and forth if u have a base or something. Just keep essentials w u as soon as u move on from one weapon/tool u throw the items required for it to free space for next upgrade. Saves time and gets u scaling faster than the game does.
5. Structures are useless - which brings me to my past point u just lose time and game diff outscales u and u die + enemies can still spawn in structures its not like it keeps them away from spawning.
Hope this helps and enjoy, overall fun game for solo and with friends :D

"Muck," created by indie developer Dani, presents itself as a survival-roguelike experience, but it is, in truth, of lacking quality in both design and execution. The gameplay is shallow, the mechanics are unrefined, and the overall experience feels more like a tech demo than a completed game. While the premise of combining survival elements with random generation is not inherently flawed, the implementation here is clumsy and inconsistent. Player progression is hindered by poor balancing, unintuitive systems, and a near-total absence of meaningful objectives.

Visually, the game is of notably poor quality. The graphics are overly simplistic, bordering on amateurish, and the user interface feels hastily put together. The aesthetic lacks identity or polish, making it difficult to distinguish whether the minimalism is intentional or simply a result of limited effort. The audio fares no better — repetitive, low-quality sound effects and a forgettable soundtrack leave the experience feeling hollow. Overall, the presentation does not support the gameplay in any significant way, and instead draws attention to the game’s shortcomings.

Multiplayer, while potentially amusing in very short bursts, does little to salvage the experience. Bugs are frequent, performance issues are common, and player cooperation often devolves into chaotic, unstructured scrambling. There is little reason to return after a single playthrough, as the game's core loop quickly becomes monotonous. "Muck" may find a niche audience due to its low price tag (being free), but even then, its entertainment value is brief at best. It ultimately fails to deliver a worthwhile or memorable experience in any meaningful capacity.

Muck is like that surprise game you stumble onto that just totally nails the mix of chaotic fun and survival challenge. It’s a survival roguelike where you gather resources, build, fight monsters, and try to stay alive—but what really makes it stand out is how goofy and unpredictable everything gets, especially when you play with friends.

The game’s art style is simple but charming, with colorful, blocky characters and a world that feels fresh every run thanks to procedural generation. You never know what kind of random monsters or weird events you’ll face, which keeps each session exciting and a little wild.

Combat is fast and fun, with a decent variety of weapons and tools to craft, plus bosses that can surprise you with their tricky patterns. The building and crafting elements give you a chance to get creative or just fortify your base for the next wave of chaos.

Why I recommend it:
If you love survival games but want something less serious and more about spontaneous fun (and hilarious moments), Muck is a great pick. It’s perfect for quick rounds or long sessions with friends, and its lighthearted vibe means you’ll laugh as much as you survive.

Dive in, get a bit messy, and enjoy the unpredictable ride. Just don’t forget to watch your back—things get wild fast! 8/10

🌅 What Is Muck?

Muck is a free-to-play survival‑roguelike developed and published solo by Dani since June 2021.

You’re stranded on a procedurally generated island where you’ve got to collect resources, craft, build bases, fight hordes, and survive—until the night (or RNG!) gets you. Its simple low-poly aesthetic hides a deceptively deep and chaotic gameplay loop.

⚔️ Gameplay & Core Mechanics

Permadeath + Roguelike Structure: Death means restarting with a new world. You lose everything—unless you use respawn statues in multiplayer. 

Day/Night Cycle: During the day, you explore, gather, and craft. At night, fierce enemies—goblins, elementals, bosses like Big Chunk and Gronk—attack in waves.

Crafting & Progression: Start with makeshift tools (rock, stick), then progress: iron → mithril → adamantite. This unlocks improved weapons, gear, bases, and furnaces.

Power-up Loot System: Slay mobs, collect coins, and open chests for random perks: life-steal, sniper scopes, jetpacks—even crazy combos. Strategic chest investments matter. 


🎉 Multiplayer Mayhem

Co‑op PvE or PvP: Up to 8 players can team up or backstab. PvP adds deception and chaos.

Tension & Humor: Balancing cooperation with trust issues, especially when betrayal is an option. “Multiplayer madness” indeed.

🎨 Visuals & Atmosphere
Low-fi Charm: Bright, blocky, stylized graphics peppered with quirky character art and eerie backgrounds. 

Memorable Audio: From serene opening notes to intense survival beats, the soundtrack is an emotional rollercoaster.

🚀 Strengths

Chaotic Fun: Fast-paced, unpredictable runs with death being part of the charm.

Free + Vast Content: Surprises with frequent updates—bosses, trader camps, new tracks, mod support. 

High Replayability: Procedural maps + randomized drops mean every run feels fresh. 

⚠️ Areas for Improvement

Brutal Difficulty/Punishing Roguelike: Quick nights and strong bosses might overwhelm newer players.

No Built-in Save for Solo: Restarts can feel rough; mods add optional saves. 

Content Depth: After mastering core loop, some players wish for even more variety. 

💡 Pro Tips

Prioritize mushrooms early—they refill hunger, stamina, and health fast. 

Open chest smartly—start low-tier early, save coins for mid-game power-ups. 

Rush mithril—it accelerates progression massively. 

Kite & strafe enemies—combat is simple but dodging is key. 

🏆 Final Verdict

Muck is a delightfully chaotic, challenging, and surprisingly deep roguelike. Its permadeath loop, quirky visuals, addictive loot, and multiplayer antics offer an experience that’s easy to jump into yet tough to master. It shines best with friends—but solo play is rewarding too. The difficulty may be steep at first, and some desire more variety, but at zero cost and packed with fun, it's a standout hidden gem in the survival genre.

If you enjoy high-stakes runs, resource grinding, randomized chaos, and friendly (or backstabbing) multiplayer—Muck is a must-play. Jump in and embrace the madness.

[b]Muck is a weirdly addictive roguelike survival game that grabs you with simple survival loops and never really lets go. You start with nothing but a stick and a torch, and from there, every night surviving by crafting, building, and exploring feels like a mini victory dance. The early days are wild and dangerous, but the progression curve is satisfyingly steep, every new upgrade or weapon feels earned through pure grit and grind.

The fast-paced nights, sudden monster ambushes, and rush to gather resources before dawn create a constant sense of tension and accomplishment. The pixel art is charming and functional, the real joy comes from that crunch of survival: chopping trees, forging armor, and hunching through darkness with nothing but ingenuity and limited supplies.

Still, Muck has its rough spots. Progression can sometimes feel grindy, especially after repeated early deaths, and the endgame boss rush gets repetitive unless you find a group with solid synergy. But for short solo sessions or frantic co-op nights with friends, Muck hits a sweet spot, a lean survival loop that’s simple to jump into, endlessly fair in its challenge, and always ready to surprise you with a night that just won’t go your way.[/b]

Ah, Muck. A name that so poetically evokes the sensation of trudging through a bog of wasted potential and half-baked ideas. One might assume—mistakenly—that a game so boldly titled would either subvert expectations with genius irony or at least offer a coherent experience beyond the aesthetic of a student’s Unity project gone rogue. Alas, Muck does neither.

To describe Muck as “minimalist” would be a gross insult to minimalism. This is not the considered restraint of a Kubrick frame or the elegant desolation of Shadow of the Colossus—this is minimalism in the way an unfinished IKEA shelf is “furniture.” The textures feel as though they were painted with the tears of forgotten polygons, and the enemy design bears all the imaginative flourish of a fever dream scribbled on a napkin at 2 a.m. by someone who just discovered what a bone is.

The gameplay loop—if one can dignify it with such terminology—consists of harvesting rocks, dying, and then asking one’s self the eternal question: why am I doing this? Combat is like watching a medieval puppet show on a caffeine crash. The AI is so devoid of logic or intent that it might be more accurate to call them weather patterns than enemies.

As for the UI? It’s not so much “user interface” as it is “user interference.” Every interaction feels like a tutorial in frustration, a deliberate exercise in reminding you that, yes, you are playing Muck, and no, you may not have joy.

Of course, one might argue that Muck is meant to be humorous—a self-aware parody of survival games. But satire, like wine, demands subtlety. Muck is not wine; it is the boxed grape juice of the gaming world, left in the sun too long and handed to you with a smug grin. Yes, we get it—it’s supposed to be bad. But intention does not excuse execution. One does not get to burn the dinner and call it deconstructed cuisine.

In conclusion, Muck is a masterclass in the art of doing the absolute least while demanding the absolute most patience. A game that dares you to find meaning in its hollow shell, and then laughs when you try. I leave this experience not enlightened, but weary. Weary, and covered in muck.

I downloaded Muck as a joke. A free game made by a YouTuber? How bad could it be?

9 hours later, I’m questioning every life decision that brought me here.

Day 1: Spawned in a field. Punched a tree. Got scared by a cow. Realized I could eat the cow. Ate the raw meat. Died.

Day 2: Learned how to craft a rock. Felt powerful. Tried to fight a goblin. Goblin made me part of the landscape.

Day 3: Found friends to play with. Big mistake. We split up to “cover more ground” — this is gamer code for “die alone in the woods.” I heard their screams echoing across the island. One of them tried to fight a dragon with a wooden axe. He was confident. He was wrong.

Somewhere along the way, we made a base out of benches and sadness. Then night fell, and the real horror began: stone goblins with the sprint speed of a Tesla and the aggression of a caffeinated goose.

Also, why are the villagers so expensive? One guy charged me 74 coins for a piece of bread. What is this, an airport?

Eventually, we summoned a boss by accident. His name was Big Chunk. We laughed at him. He did not laugh back.

10/10.

It’s free. It’s chaotic. It’s got more heart than some AAA titles.
I came for the meme. I stayed because I was too afraid to alt+F4.

Will I survive to day 10?
Unlikely.
But I’ll Muck around and find out.

Really fun especially with friends, the first 10-20 rounds will remain fresh enough to entertain. Past that point you know how the game works and any further enjoyment is from intentionally challenging yourself, for example by getting the achievements. Those are kind of ridiculous btw, not impossible damn they're difficult. You'll probably need to cheese them if you don't want to get a phd in the game.

The game is lowkey a roguelike, mixed with a survival game. It's all very basic, you'll probably find every material and every monster within 5 hours (besides the more complicated sword crafts which are still fairly simple)

You can run and store this on a low end 2010 laptop, probably. At least any pc that was built within the last 10 years will never struggle.

The "powerscaling" is the one biggest problem I have. As the day count increases, enemies gain increased attack and hp (you can see the exact multiplier with debug mode). It's calibrated in a way that never makes you actually be stronger than them, except from legendary perk stacking blowing everything up. But stats-wise, you will never tank them much longer than the previous night, or kill them in one hit without sniper scope.

Overall a fun little game to play with friends every so often, but not the type of game you can play for that long. (my 50 hours crush every other friend I have and that's not even high. Since it's free and a tiny download, I still think it's great.

Dani’s Muck is an unapologetically chaotic blend of survival mechanics, roguelike intensity, and cooperative mayhem. It thrives on an endearing mix of absurdity and genuine challenge, making it an experience that is as frustrating as it is addictively rewarding.

At its core, Muck starts with the familiar survival game formula: gather resources, craft tools, and build shelter before nightfall. However, it quickly sets itself apart with an escalating difficulty curve that transforms the game into a frantic battle for survival. The procedural generation ensures that no two runs are identical, while the combat—against bizarre yet terrifying enemies—adds a relentless pressure that keeps players on their toes.

Visually, Muck embraces a minimalist yet effective aesthetic, opting for a clean and functional style that prioritizes gameplay fluidity. The soundtrack, with its energetic and sometimes comically intense beats, complements the game’s unpredictable nature, heightening the sense of urgency as the sun sets and monstrosities emerge.

Perhaps Muck’s greatest strength lies in its cooperative multiplayer. What starts as a casual resource-gathering session often devolves into frantic shouting as waves of enemies storm the group’s fragile encampments. The balance between camaraderie and sheer chaos makes for an experience that is equal parts hilarious and demanding.

Despite its intentionally rough edges—reflecting Dani’s signature style of rapid, community-driven development—Muck is a testament to how creativity and game design fundamentals can come together to craft an experience that is both deeply engaging and delightfully absurd. It may not take itself too seriously, but therein lies its charm. A must-try for fans of roguelikes and survival games alike.

Muck, developed by Dani, is a wonderfully chaotic and highly addictive survival game that blends simplicity with engaging mechanics, resulting in an experience that is both challenging and rewarding. From the moment you start, you’re thrown into a vibrant world full of danger, but also incredible opportunities for fun and growth. It’s an exciting journey that you’ll want to return to again and again.

The core of Muck’s appeal is its unique combination of survival and crafting. You start with nothing but a rock and must gather resources to build tools, weapons, and structures, all while fending off increasingly dangerous enemies that come at night. The game brilliantly balances the rush of resource gathering with the intense pressure of surviving against waves of enemies. The progression feels very rewarding, as you unlock new items and abilities, all while improving your base and pushing the limits of your survival skills.

One of the standout features of Muck is its dynamic difficulty. Every new session feels different, thanks to random world generation and the constant threat of increasingly difficult waves of enemies. This keeps the game fresh, making every playthrough feel unique. There’s a constant sense of progression and challenge, especially as you try to improve with each new attempt, learning from your mistakes. Whether you’re playing solo or with friends in multiplayer mode, the experience is equally intense and fun.

Visually, Muck has a charming, low-poly aesthetic that is both pleasing and fitting for the chaotic nature of the gameplay. The colorful environments are full of personality, and the enemies, though simple in design, are memorable and add a unique character to the world. It’s a bright, welcoming world that hides a lot of danger beneath its colorful surface, adding to the thrill.

The music and sound design are excellent, with a soundtrack that fits the adventurous spirit of the game. It changes in intensity depending on the time of day or the current threats, heightening the tension during the night and making every victory feel earned. The sounds of your tools, weapons, and enemies add a layer of immersion, making each resource gathering session or combat encounter more satisfying.

But perhaps what makes Muck truly special is the way it encourages teamwork and creativity. If you play with friends, you’ll quickly find yourselves strategizing, sharing resources, and building massive structures to defend yourselves. It’s the kind of game where each session can turn into a hilarious and frantic experience, full of memorable moments. The ability to play with up to 10 players ensures that no matter your group size, you can experience the chaos and excitement together.

In conclusion, Muck is a brilliant and enjoyable survival game that doesn’t take itself too seriously, but still delivers a satisfying and challenging experience. Its blend of resource management, combat, and random elements ensures that every session is a new adventure. Whether you're in it for the solo grind or the fun of multiplayer chaos, Muck is an exhilarating ride that will keep you coming back for more.

These type of achievements that of force you to have friends can be really annoying and seem undoable because how are you going to find 8 other people who want to play this game and will dedicated enough time to get skilled enough to complete the achievement conditions?

Overall, this game is a blast and created some great memories with friends.

I recommend playing it!

Navigating the treacherous terrain of Muck is like trying to knit a sweater with a greased-up squirrel – it's a wild, unpredictable ride! This game has got it all: the thrill of the hunt for resources, the joy of crafting your base from the ground up, and the heart-pounding action of fending off whatever nasties the roguish world throws at you. The open world is a candy store for explorers, and the multiplayer mode adds a layer of camaraderie (or sabotage, if that's your thing). While the lack of a save-load system can be a sticking point, the overall experience is as rich and satisfying as a well-crafted pie – minus the calories, of course. So, if you're looking for a survival challenge with a side of personality, Muck is the game for you!

[b] I just wanted to say, this game was more fun than I expected. Yes its jank, and has some issues here it there, but that made me ask. How do I break this game in a way that will let me beat this rogue like game?  [/b]

[h1] Chapter: How I beat the game [/h1]

 [h2] The Beginning - playing on normal [/h2]
Started off by playing normally. Figuring out the upgrade paths and what material can mine which resource. But we would always die on day 4 to 6 for various reasons. It was very difficult to play the game "normally" felt like i didn't have money, more power ups, not enough food, not enough progression through the metal tier system.

[h2] The Village [/h2]
Then we discovered the village. And then we learned that each village has a random assortment of traders that sell items. Some of those items are adamantite items that cost 75 gold. The goal then became, how fast could we find a village first and find a merchant that sold an adamantite tool. One of the first fast ways i thought of breaking the game is by selling the villagers wooden tools for 5 gold. However, due to the coding of the game, if you had 2 wooden axes in your inventory, and you sold the axe for 5 gold, both axes would disappear in your inventory and you will receive 5 gold instead of 10. So the tech became, how fast I could craft axes at a workbench next to the merchant and hit the sell button. 
By doing this, we were able to buy both an adamantite axe and pickaxe usually before the second or third night. 
We still died to boss on 4th night. Then we learned that we could make an obamium sword that did more damage than an adamantite sword. 
We still kept dieing to the boss on the 4th night since we either lacked armor, food, and skill, as well as powerups; since all our money was funneled into purchasing adamantite tools instead of opening chests. We opened the black chests though since they were free to open up.

We were then on a race for time. We would try to find a village that sold an adamantite pick and axe and sold obamium on day 1, and if we did not find a good village, we would reset. and we would try to get obamium swords by day 3, and power up using the square challenge totems on day 4. Sometimes we would make it, sometimes we would get projectiles hit by the ads spawning at night while the boss is active. 

[h2] Stealing what is not nailed down [/h2]
I then started experimenting with the game solo. When I then found out some major breakthroughs that would save time. I learned that in villages, the villagers would only attack you in 2 scenerios, 1 is that if you attack them or that they run infront of you mining or chopping wood and 2, if you interact/open the chief chest. All other chests and structures are free game.

[h2] New Game Plan [/h2]
The gameplan changed to day 1, find village with adamantite tools. loot all the chests except cheif chests and hopefully you found a wooden axe in the chests. Then use the wooden axe to break all the barrels in the village for money. And sell Wheat to the food vendor if possible to get the rest of the money to afford an adamantite tool before night fell on day 1.

Another break though that i discovered was that you could break the chief chest with an axe to obtain the contents inside without angering the villagers which yielded usually gold ingots which could be converted into gold coins and a weapon piece. 

[h1] The god run [/h1]
[h2]seed: -473123428 [/h2]
This is the random seed that I got where a village was right in front of me and sold both an adamantite pick and axe. Although there is no person selling obamium, we have the tools to go mine it.
I was able to get adamantite axe before night 1. 
obamium sword before night 2.
powered up with challenge totems before and during night 3
made a full set of obamium armout before the night of the 4th along side with gathering resources for the ship. 

Then came the guardian battles. Once you learned not to jump during the attacks, you can easily walk out of the telegraphed red marker aoe. A trick that i found was that for its beam attack, you can just stand behind a tree or just placed down a wall to have it LOS you. Once all the gems were collected and resources need to fix the ship were acquired and placed onto the ship. I was able to set sail and was free!........

[b] Finally while lavished in victory, I uninstalled the game, never to be played again. Thank you to the god seed that i found. Amazing game for being a solo dev and making it free. I had a good time, and I wont be coming back. TY for the fun memories. [/b]

Why Muck is Unbalanced and Stressful

Muck is a video game created by youtuber, Dani. It’s a survival game that’s extremely unbalanced when it comes to the mechanics. Heres why.

Before the you-know-who update

Simple Enemy Problems

Now, starting simple, the game is way too hard already just on EASY MODE. The first instinct of the player is to build shelter. This clueless player has no way to know that the shelter will be destroyed in seconds. Second instinct, no base. Enemies will destroy the base and kill the player since their unprepared. Third instinct, sky base. The problem here is that they won't know that they need to get up BEFORE night, or the enemies will destroy the whole thing. You can say “oh just use poles as a base!” The problem is, Small Chunk, and a certain you-know-who we will get too soon. Small chunk throws rocks, meaning that the player will have to build either extremely high or get lucky. The problem we keep seeing is that there's no guide for the player to follow, thus causing them to assume what they must do, based on other games. This is just scratching the surface; we have much more to talk about.

Armor and Weapons

Getting armor and weapons in Muck is a nightmare. You need to get wood with a rock, craft a table, craft a pickaxe and axe, mine rocks, craft a furnace, mine iron, smelt the iron, craft an iron pickaxe and axe, mine mithril, craft mithril gear, and that’s the armor tier just below the final. Remember that you must do this while like every 5 minutes it turns night, enemies bombard your base, and you could even die in the process. Also note that there’s no saving the game, respawning, and it’s basically Minecraft Hardcore if you're playing alone. Now this entire time I've been leaving a certain someone out, so let's talk about him.

G R O N K


 Muck is unbalanced and way too confusing for new players, 
And then there's this... Thing. This thing is way stronger than Big Chunk but has spawned first in EVERY playthrough of mine. This could be a glitch with Easy Mode, but this stupid rat has ruined EVERY SINGLE run I've done with my friend. Were just Chilin, day 6, and suddenly THIS GUY spawns and kills us. He deals too much damage, comes when the player is unprepared, and there's no way to know when hes about to spawn. Take Terraria for example. You get text whenever a boss is about to spawn naturally. Note also that you can learn from your mistake since you respawn. Muck? It just spawns on Day 6 or Day 7 instantly. Progress in Muck is way too stressful, mostly because of this goblin degenerate. Now, combine this with everything else. Slow progress due to enemies and ore smelting times, something I didn’t even mention, Stamina and Food, no respawning, and then right after this guy. This is why Muck is just difficult to play. This is on EASY MODE, by the way.

Conclusion

Muck needs to be made more balanced, or the game will simply remain too difficult. If you're reading this, Dani, I would suggest making progress faster, and giving more time to prepare for bosses and maybe longer days, since night happens extremely quickly. Thus concludes my essay on why Muck is unbalanced, . Thanks for reading, and Wishlist Karlson on Steam!

Muck. Oh, Muck. You beautiful, brutal, and utterly addictive beast of a game. My journey through your procedurally generated world was a trial by fire, a symphony of pain punctuated by the sweet, sweet clang of newly forged weapons.

I died. A lot. Skeletons, goblins, even the trees seemed to have it out for me. Each death was a lesson learned, each respawn a renewed vow of vengeance. I slowly clawed my way up the food chain, from shivering, naked newbie to a (somewhat) hardened survivor, decked out in glistening armor and wielding weapons that would make Thor jealous.

And then, the Big Boss. The final showdown.  After countless attempts, heart-pounding near-deaths, and a string of curses that would make a sailor blush, I emerged victorious.  Relief washed over me, followed by a profound sense of accomplishment... and exhaustion. "Never again," I swore, "I'm done with this masochistic masterpiece."

But here's the thing about Muck. It sinks its hooks into you. Days after my "final" victory, I find myself drawn back to its simplistic charm, the allure of another run, another chance to prove my dominance over its unforgiving world.  Maybe just one more time...

If you're looking for a challenging, rewarding, and surprisingly addictive survival game, Muck is it. Just be prepared to die. A lot.

A Chaotic Adventure in Survival Mode
Muck is one of those games where you think, "How hard can it be?" – only to find out that the game loves to yank the rug out from under you and let a troll smack you in the face. Here's my detailed review:

Positive Aspects:
Adrenaline Rush Guaranteed: Muck delivers an adrenaline rush you won't forget. The tension that builds as the sun sets and monsters emerge is fantastic. It's like a horror-comedy where you want to laugh and scream at the same time.

Survival Instinct Required: This game demands your survival instinct. You have to gather resources, craft weapons, and fend off an ever-growing threat. It's a bit like "Survival of the Fittest" – only you're usually not the fittest.

Randomly Generated Worlds: Each game world is randomly generated, meaning no two sessions are the same. There are always new challenges and surprises waiting for you.

Multiplayer Fun: The game is even more fun in co-op mode with friends. Surviving together, gathering resources, and fighting off hordes of monsters – it's a chaotic fest.

Charming Graphics: The simple yet charming graphics give the game a unique look. It's like Minecraft on extreme difficulty.

Negative Aspects:
Brutal Difficulty: The difficulty level is brutal. Just when you think you've built a decent base and gathered enough resources, trolls come along and wreck everything. It's almost masochistic, but in a funny way.

Unpredictable Dangers: The dangers in the game are as unpredictable as April weather. Suddenly, monsters appear and chase you relentlessly. It's like the game is waiting to ambush you around every corner.

Short Days, Long Nights: Days are short and hectic, while nights feel like an eternity. The monsters seem to be waiting for sunset to make your life miserable.

Resource Scarcity: Sometimes it feels like you spend more time searching for resources than actually building or fighting. It can be frustrating when you're hunting for a specific resource for hours.

Laughable Deaths: The deaths in this game are often so absurd that you can't help but laugh. One wrong step, a failed jump, or an unexpected attack – and you're dead. But hey, at least you die with style.

Conclusion:
Muck is a chaotic adventure that offers both challenges and plenty of laughs. The extreme difficulty and unpredictable dangers make it a game you both love and hate. It's like a rollercoaster ride – you never know what's coming next, but it's definitely fun. So grab your friends, face the challenge, and get ready to die often and laugh even more!

The game deserves better... both balancing-wise and also content-wise.
To put it simply, the game is a constant scramble for how you will survive the next night (aka, every like.. 5 minutes).

A few issues me and my buddy had with the game:
1. We never knew when we were properly prepared for certain challenges, ending in us dying.
2. The game expects you to be a high-octane speedrunner in order to be prepared in time for its mandatory difficulty increases and natural boss spawns.
3. The enemies in the game are super overpowered (even on the first night), and there is no possible way to hide or flee from them as they constantly follow you until you either kill them or die.
4. Lastly, the game claims to be a "rogue-like", when rogue-likes typically have you grow after each death in some way, whereas in this game you are thrown into the same exact hellhole as the last.

To kinda summarize the game, it is a fun game for messing around with friends for about 15 minutes, other than that you need to be a sweaty speedrunning god gamer in order to get any accomplishment at all before inevitably dying to a random goblin on night 2.

Muck is a great Indie game, but Dark Souls 2 is better, and a quick guide on growing carrots in your backyard.

Muck is a standout indie game that successfully blends survival, exploration, and humor. With a unique art style and a focus on cooperative gameplay, the game challenges players to gather resources, craft tools, and defend themselves from waves of enemies. The game's simple mechanics, such as chopping down trees for wood or mining for ore, create a satisfying loop that keeps players engaged. Its difficulty ramps up as you progress, and the occasional chaotic moments where enemies overwhelm your defenses bring a fun sense of tension. The random generation of maps and enemies ensures that every playthrough feels fresh and exciting. With its blend of action and strategy, Muck offers an enjoyable and often unpredictable experience, particularly when played with friends.

Dark Souls 2: The Pinnacle of Gaming

However, while Muck is a fun and engaging indie experience, it can’t compare to the grandeur and depth of Dark Souls 2. Dark Souls 2 takes the formula of its predecessors and refines it, delivering one of the best action RPGs ever made. The game's combat is methodical, requiring precision and strategy, with each enemy encounter feeling meaningful and rewarding. The world of Dark Souls 2 is vast and interconnected, filled with intricate design, hidden secrets, and an atmosphere that pulls you into its dark and dangerous world. Unlike Muck, where you mainly gather resources and fight waves of enemies, Dark Souls 2 focuses on exploration, mastery, and overcoming tough, memorable bosses. The depth of its world-building, the challenge of its combat, and the satisfaction of progression make it a far more engaging and long-lasting experience than Muck.

Why Dark Souls 2 is the Better Choice

While Muck provides a fun and accessible gameplay loop, Dark Souls 2 offers a deeper, more immersive experience that rewards patience, skill, and exploration. The sense of accomplishment in Dark Souls 2 is incomparable, as every hard-fought victory feels earned, and every discovery is part of a larger, interconnected world. Muck is certainly an enjoyable game, especially for those looking for a casual survival experience, but it lacks the complexity and emotional weight that Dark Souls 2 brings. If you're looking for a game that challenges you in every sense and provides a rich, rewarding experience, Dark Souls 2 is the game you should be playing.

Carrots are root vegetables that grow from seeds planted in loose, well-drained soil. To grow carrots, you begin by sowing the seeds directly into the soil in early spring or late summer, depending on your climate. The seeds should be planted about 1/4 inch deep and spaced several inches apart to allow room for the roots to grow. Carrots need plenty of sunlight and consistent moisture, so regular watering is important. Over time, the seeds sprout into thin green tops, and the edible carrot roots begin to develop underground. As they grow, it's important to thin out the plants to ensure the remaining carrots have enough space to mature. After a few months, the carrots are ready to harvest when the tops start to appear above the soil.

If you aren't even going to try to make a good game, then don't make a game. Simple as that.

The combat consists exclusively of hopping around like a canola oil droplet on an iron skillet and poking at enemies, watching helplessly as your food and stamina bars drain faster than senior's bank account when their deadbeat children steal their information.

Give it four in-game day cycles and you will get one shot by an enemy that does enough damage to nullify the full set of adamantite armor you sweated your butt off to grind out.

I always appreciate when an indie developer puts their heart into their work and creates an experience that AAA developers have long since abandoned the art of. It is no obscurity that some of the best games in recent memory, such as FNAF, Warframe, and Path of Exile, were created by small teams united by one vision. This game is not crafted with the same intent. It is a contrivance put forth by a person who regurgitated the same rougelike mechanics we've seen in every single offering to the genre, but with sillyquirky Gen Z item descriptions and laughably poor scaling relative to the massively overtuned hordes of bosses who will turn you inside out no matter how hard you race to empower your character.

A lot of people are saying the combat is too hard or the game is too grindy but I disagree. The game is meant to be frustrating, the achievement for opening the game is literally called "big mistake" and if you manage your time well in game then you can get quiet far in the game decently fast, and although there is a lot to do it doesn't get boring. It's actually very fun to play for me but my problem is that you cannot save. Although it's not grindy, it still takes time to progress and since there is no saving you can't just play the game over multiple days like with pretty much every other survival game. Minecraft or Terraria don't expect you to beat the game in one go, so they let you press "save and quit" so you can go back to the game later when you have time. But here you have to complete it all in one go and if you die there is no respawning, voiding all your progress and forcing you to start over. If you play with friends you can revive each other but if you both die then you obviously can't do that and you need to start again. I don't have a problem with games that take a lot of time to complete but here I need to spend multiple hours straight and if I get caught off guard then I die and have to start over again. I'm happy for the 90% of people who rated this game positive on steam but I can't find this game enjoyable if the barrier of entry is spending several hours straight playing this game. If the game let you save so you could spend like an hour playing per day instead of having to beat the game in one go I would definable rate this game positive but there don't seem to be signs of that happening anytime soon.

Muck. Just the name alone stirs something deep within the gaming soul. If you're still unfamiliar with this masterpiece, allow me to enlighten you: Muck isn't just a game—it's an experience. A test of willpower, a battle against the clock, and perhaps most importantly, an embodiment of all the pure chaos that modern gaming is capable of.

Developed by the genius behind Demon Slayer: The Muckening (okay, I may have made that up), Muck combines the thrill of survival, the joy of multiplayer mayhem, and just a hint of that secret sauce that makes you want to hit "Restart" for the fifth time after you’ve died in the most ridiculous way possible. But that's part of the charm. Each death feels like an opportunity for growth, and the sense of progression is palpable—even if it's just the fleeting hope that maybe, this time, you'll make it past the first 10 minutes.

Let’s talk about the gameplay for a second: It’s simple—but not too simple. The mechanics are straightforward enough to keep anyone engaged, but there’s enough depth to satisfy even the most seasoned of survival game players. You start with nothing, gather resources, craft weapons, and survive waves of increasingly savage enemies. It's like Minecraft meets Dark Souls—but with more hilarious deaths, confusing weapon choices, and a general sense of "what on Earth is happening?"

But here’s where Muck truly earns its place as the BEST game ever:

The community. If you’ve ever played Muck, you’ve seen the memes. The low taper fade meme has become almost as iconic as the game itself. For some reason, Muck has become synonymous with that image of a gamer sporting the low taper fade haircut. It’s the perfect blend of cringe and comedy that fits the chaotic vibe of Muck perfectly. You can’t escape it. And honestly? You wouldn’t want to.

Imagine, if you will, a group of friends playing Muck, trying to survive against a relentless onslaught of monsters, and then—out of nowhere—one of them pops into the chat with the phrase: “Low taper fade?” It’s like a rite of passage. If you know, you know. It’s both a meme and an inside joke that’s somehow become a part of the Muck universe. It’s honestly hilarious how often the low taper fade meme pops up while you're furiously crafting a pickaxe and trying to fend off an army of goblins. And somehow, it makes the whole experience that much better.

In conclusion, Muck isn’t just the BEST game ever—it’s a cultural phenomenon. It’s fun, it’s frustrating, it’s funny, and it’s full of surprises. Whether you’re dodging boulders, crafting axes, or getting absolutely destroyed by monsters (or your own teammates), Muck will have you laughing all the way to your next low taper fade meme. This game is pure, unfiltered chaos—and that’s why we love it.

Muck: An In-Depth Review

Introduction

Muck, developed by Dani, is a rogue-like survival game that combines elements of crafting, combat, and exploration in a procedurally generated world. Released in June 2021, Muck quickly gained attention for its engaging mechanics and distinctive style. The game invites players to fend for themselves in a world that becomes increasingly hostile as they progress. This review will delve into the core aspects of Muck, including its gameplay, graphics, content, and overall experience.

Gameplay Mechanics

Muck revolves around survival and progression in a procedurally generated world that changes each time you play. The game blends crafting, combat, and exploration, offering a challenging and dynamic experience.

1. Survival and Crafting:
   - Gathering Resources: Players start with nothing and must gather resources from the environment. This includes chopping trees, mining rocks, and hunting animals for food. Resource collection is crucial for crafting tools, weapons, and building structures.
   - Crafting System: The crafting system in Muck is straightforward but effective. Players can craft a range of items, from basic tools to advanced weapons and armor. The recipes are unlocked as players progress and explore, encouraging experimentation and discovery.

2. Combat and Enemies:
   - Combat Mechanics: The combat system in Muck is engaging, though it leans towards the basic side. Players use a variety of weapons and tools to fend off enemies. Combat is generally fast-paced and requires players to be strategic in their approach.
   - Enemy Types: The game features a variety of enemies, each with different behaviors and attack patterns. Some enemies are relatively simple to defeat, while others present a significant challenge. The variety ensures that players must adapt their strategies to handle different threats.

3. Exploration and Environment:
   - Procedural Generation: The world of Muck is procedurally generated, meaning that each playthrough offers a new layout and set of challenges. This keeps the game fresh and encourages exploration.
   - Biomes and Structures: As players explore, they encounter different biomes, each with unique resources and challenges. The game also features various structures and points of interest that provide opportunities for loot and exploration.

Graphics and Art Style

Muck employs a simplistic, blocky art style reminiscent of early indie games and sandbox titles. The graphics are functional and convey the game's aesthetic without being overly complex. This design choice aligns with the game's indie roots and contributes to its charm.

- Visuals: The visual style is deliberately minimalist, which helps in maintaining performance and focusing on gameplay mechanics. While not graphically intensive, the art style fits well with the game's overall vibe and contributes to its unique character.

- Performance: The game generally performs well on a range of systems. Its modest graphical demands mean that even players with lower-end hardware can enjoy a smooth experience. However, as with many procedurally generated games, performance can vary depending on the complexity of the generated world.

Content and Replayability

Muck offers a substantial amount of content, with a focus on replayability and procedural generation. Key aspects include:

- Campaign and Objectives: The game features a series of objectives and challenges that players can undertake. These range from building specific structures to defeating powerful bosses. The open-ended nature of the game allows players to approach these objectives in various ways.

- Replayability: The procedural generation of the game world ensures that each playthrough is different. This, combined with the variety of crafting options, enemies, and biomes, contributes to a high level of replayability. Players are encouraged to experiment with different strategies and approaches, which adds to the game's longevity.

- Multiplayer: Muck supports multiplayer, allowing players to team up and tackle the game's challenges together. This cooperative mode adds an additional layer of enjoyment and complexity, as players must coordinate their efforts to survive and progress.

Community and Support

Muck has a growing community of players and modders who contribute to the game's ecosystem. The developer, Dani, has shown a commitment to supporting and updating the game based on player feedback. This includes addressing bugs, balancing gameplay, and adding new content.

- Modding: The game’s modding community is active, with players creating custom content and modifications. This adds to the game's replayability and allows for a more personalized experience.

- Updates and Feedback: The developer has been responsive to community feedback, releasing updates that address issues and introduce new features. This ongoing support is a positive aspect of the game's development.

Conclusion

Muck is a compelling survival game that offers a blend of crafting, combat, and exploration in a procedurally generated world. Its straightforward mechanics, combined with its distinctive art style and replayability, make it an enjoyable experience for fans of the genre.

While the game may not have the depth of some larger titles, its focus on survival and crafting, along with its cooperative multiplayer mode, provides a satisfying experience. The procedural generation ensures that each playthrough is unique, keeping the game fresh and engaging.

For players who enjoy indie survival games with a focus on crafting and exploration, Muck is a worthwhile title that delivers a fun and challenging experience. Its simplicity, combined with its engaging mechanics and supportive community, make it a notable entry in the genre.

Game is fun, and if it weren't for some of the worse balance I've seen in years I'd happily recommend it, but if you aren't going in knowing how to speedrun progression you're gonna be getting 1 shotted by the vast majority of enemies pretty quickly. Without mods there is no ability to save your game, and likewise if you do die your save is immediately wiped and you get to go start again.

It's a great foundation, but 3 years in and being one of the most (unfair) challenging games I've played in years, outdoing the Souls games, is a miracle. Tutorial ending at "Pick up a rock and hit a tree" doesn't help, either.

Thus far my furthest run has been I think day 6, with some good gear and a really solid start for progressing towards harder bosses and big kid stuff, only to have one of the most obnoxious enemies I've ever seen in gaming spawn in 2 feet away from me at night, nearly 1 shot me with a pinpoint accurate laser beam and then chase me quite literally across the map to kill me. Sure wish enemies didn't see you once and decide that you're the only thing in the universe worth hurting from then on. Being able to run away and resupply without being hit in the back would be great, but as is you either kill the enemy or die. There is no loss of aggro, and that is kinda the final nail in the coffin for me.

Having read through other reviews I feel like they're either bot accounts or paid for, because seeing the game's difficulty curve being described as "Strategic" and the progression called "Deep and interesting" is so far from the truth it's not even funny.

 It's discount Rust, but if you aren't fully kitted by your third in-game day it won't be players raiding you, but rather NPCs deciding your free trial of life has ended. The AI is the dumbest I've seen in gaming almost ever, 99% of them being susceptible to being circle strafed to death and as a result they make up for that by going from doing basically 0 damage to snapping their fingers and having you melt.

Fake reviews aside, I pray that some day a game like this is released and actually worked on to make it balanced and fun in equal measure, because this ain't it.

Also, one final note: Why is grass demonstrably harmful to the game experience? Not being able to see anything on the ground literally ever, especially when grass is on by default, is remarkably short sighted.
