"Muck": A Masterpiece of Indie Game Design
"Muck" is an indie game that defies all expectations and delivers an experience far greater than the sum of its parts. Developed by the YouTuber Dani, this game has quickly become a standout title in the survival genre, captivating players with its addictive gameplay, charming visuals, and innovative design. What began as a fun side project has blossomed into a masterpiece that showcases the power of creativity, community-driven development, and pure, unadulterated fun.

At its core, "Muck" is a survival game that combines elements of crafting, exploration, and combat. However, what sets it apart from the multitude of other games in the genre is its perfect balance of challenge and reward. From the moment you start collecting resources and building your base, you're hooked. The game offers a continuous loop of gathering materials, crafting tools, and defending against waves of enemies that keeps you on your toes and always eager to see what comes next.

One of the most impressive aspects of "Muck" is its depth. Despite its simple premise, the game offers a surprisingly rich experience with a variety of gameplay mechanics that are easy to pick up but difficult to master. The procedural generation of the world ensures that no two playthroughs are ever the same, giving the game incredible replayability. The combat is fast-paced and satisfying, with a variety of weapons and enemies that require different strategies to defeat. The crafting system is intuitive yet complex, allowing players to create everything from basic tools to powerful weapons and structures.

"Muck" also shines in its visual and audio design. The graphics, while minimalist, are charming and perfectly suited to the game's tone. The vibrant colors and simple, blocky style give the game a unique aesthetic that is both nostalgic and fresh. The soundtrack, composed of catchy tunes and atmospheric tracks, complements the gameplay perfectly, enhancing the overall experience.

What truly makes "Muck" a standout title, however, is the sense of community it has fostered. The game was born out of a joke on Dani's YouTube channel, and its development has been heavily influenced by player feedback and suggestions. This collaborative approach has resulted in a game that feels like it was made by gamers, for gamers. The developer's commitment to listening to the community and regularly updating the game with new content and features has only strengthened its appeal and longevity.

In conclusion, "Muck" is an extraordinary achievement in indie game development. It takes a genre that has been done to death and breathes new life into it with creativity, charm, and a deep understanding of what makes games fun. Whether you're a fan of survival games or just looking for something new and exciting to play, "Muck" is an absolute must-play. It's a shining example of how passion and community can come together to create something truly special, and it deserves every bit of the praise it has received. <3

This may look like a wacky Minecraft clone (which it is) but it is not only that, this was a surprisingly challenging experience that will make you question what a “hard” game has to be. Let me run you through the game.

You get dropped into the world with no objective said, but instead your exploration is the progress towards the objectives which ultimately is to leave the island. You do this with the help of a boat that you have to repair through collecting wood, flowers, maybe kill a boss or… five. This may sound mild but I must remind you that there are no respawns so if you die you have to restart on another seed, plus you don’t have a lot of health most of the time so this is already challenging. Another point is that the difficulty modes are quite literally DIFFICULTy modes, easy is hard, medium is lethal, hard is realism. You go down in three hits and there is no real party or block or dodge system. This plus the fact that every five night they spawn a boss on you makes the game seriously difficult to finish thanks to the simplicity. This is the charm with the game, soulsikes have the charm of being hard but also having complex armour and magic systems meanwhile muck is so simple that it wouldn’t really make much of a difference in what weapons you use, because it will be hard no matter what. This is what gives the feeling of complexity to a simple game and the truth is that you could slap a 10$ price tag on this and nobody would bat an eye. The fun part? Title: Adventures in Muck: Bonding Through Gooning

In the realm of online gaming, where worlds collide and challenges abound, there exists a unique camaraderie forged between siblings. This essay delves into the exhilarating adventures of two brothers, navigating the chaotic yet thrilling landscape of the game "Muck" while engaging in a playful rivalry known fondly as gooning.

"Muck," a survival game set in a procedurally generated world, provides the perfect backdrop for competitive and cooperative gameplay alike. As the brothers embark on their virtual journey, armed with nothing but wit and determination, their dynamic unfolds into a symphony of laughter, strategy, and occasional mischief.

The essence of gooning lies in the art of playful sabotage and good-natured taunting. Each brother, driven by a mix of sibling rivalry and mutual respect, finds ingenious ways to thwart the other's progress. Whether it's hiding essential resources, triggering in-game traps, or crafting ludicrously oversized weapons just for laughs, every encounter becomes a testament to their shared bond.

Amidst the chaos, however, lies a deeper connection. The brothers' banter and friendly competition serve as a channel for communication and understanding. Through their gooning antics, they learn to anticipate each other's moves, collaborate more effectively during challenges, and celebrate victories as a team.

In "Muck," survival hinges not only on individual skill but also on teamwork. The brothers quickly realize that their gooning escapades, while amusing, often lead to unexpected moments of synergy. A failed prank may inadvertently save a teammate from a lurking enemy, or a competitive chase through the wilderness might uncover a hidden cache of rare items, benefiting both parties.

Beyond the virtual realm, their experiences in "Muck" mirror the dynamics of real-life relationships. The game becomes a playground where they explore different facets of camaraderie—supporting each other through setbacks, celebrating achievements together, and learning to navigate challenges as a unified force.

As their adventures in "Muck" unfold, the brothers discover a profound truth: gooning is not merely about one-upmanship but about forging memories and strengthening bonds. The game serves as a canvas where they paint their unique story of sibling rivalry intertwined with mutual affection. Each session becomes a chapter in their shared narrative, filled with inside jokes, epic battles, and the occasional mishap that becomes a cherished tale in family lore.

In conclusion, "Muck" is more than just a game to these brothers; it's a canvas for their shared experiences and a testament to the enduring bond between siblings. Through gooning, they navigate the challenges of the virtual world with laughter and camaraderie, forging memories that will last a lifetime. As they continue their adventures, one thing remains certain: whether they're gooning on each other or conquering formidable foes, their journey in "Muck" is a testament to the power of gaming to bring people closer together.

"Muck" is a delightful surprise in the realm of survival sandbox games, offering a refreshingly simple yet addictively challenging experience. Developed by a solo indie developer, this game captures the essence of survival with its blend of crafting, exploration, and relentless combat against hordes of enemies.

At first glance, "Muck" may appear deceptively straightforward with its voxel-based graphics and basic mechanics. However, beneath its minimalist exterior lies a deep and engaging gameplay loop. Players start stranded on an island and must gather resources, craft tools and weapons, and build shelters to survive against increasingly difficult waves of enemies that come at night.

What sets "Muck" apart is its procedurally generated world, which ensures no two playthroughs are alike. Each session offers a new challenge, pushing you to adapt your strategies and utilize the environment to your advantage. The pacing is brisk, with a constant sense of progression as you gather stronger materials and unlock new crafting recipes.

The game encourages exploration with its diverse biomes, each harboring unique resources and dangers. From lush forests to icy tundras and volcanic landscapes, every area demands careful navigation and resource management. The variety keeps gameplay engaging and ensures there's always something new to discover.

Combat in "Muck" is surprisingly satisfying, requiring quick reflexes and strategic positioning to fend off swarms of enemies. Boss encounters further ramp up the challenge, testing your preparation and teamwork if playing with friends.

While "Muck" excels in many aspects, it does have a few rough edges typical of indie titles. Some may find the learning curve steep initially, especially with minimal in-game tutorials. Additionally, the solo developer's constraints mean updates and optimizations may not come as quickly as larger studio releases.

In conclusion, "Muck" is a testament to the creativity and passion of indie game development. It's a game that grows on you, offering a compelling blend of survival, exploration, and challenging gameplay. If you're a fan of sandbox survival games and enjoy the thrill of overcoming increasingly tough odds, "Muck" is definitely worth diving into.

Anyway, here's a brownie recipe;

Ingredients
185g unsalted butter
185g best dark chocolate
85g plain flour
40g cocoa powder
50g white chocolate
50g milk chocolate
3 large eggs
275g golden caster sugar

Method
STEP 1
Cut 185g unsalted butter into small cubes and tip into a medium bowl. Break 185g dark chocolate into small pieces and drop into the bowl.

STEP 2
Fill a small saucepan about a quarter full with hot water, then sit the bowl on top so it rests on the rim of the pan, not touching the water. Put over a low heat until the butter and chocolate have melted, stirring occasionally to mix them.

STEP 3
Remove the bowl from the pan. Alternatively, cover the bowl loosely with cling film and put in the microwave for 2 minutes on High. Leave the melted mixture to cool to room temperature.

STEP 4
While you wait for the chocolate to cool, position a shelf in the middle of your oven and turn the oven on to 180C/160C fan/gas 4.

STEP 5
Using a shallow 20cm square tin, cut out a square of non-stick baking parchment to line the base. Tip 85g plain flour and 40g cocoa powder into a sieve held over a medium bowl. Tap and shake the sieve so they run through together and you get rid of any lumps.

STEP 6
Chop 50g white chocolate and 50g milk chocolate into chunks on a board.

STEP 7
Break 3 large eggs into a large bowl and tip in 275g golden caster sugar. With an electric mixer on maximum speed, whisk the eggs and sugar. They will look thick and creamy, like a milk shake. This can take 3-8 minutes, depending on how powerful your mixer is. You’ll know it’s ready when the mixture becomes really pale and about double its original volume. Another check is to turn off the mixer, lift out the beaters and wiggle them from side to side. If the mixture that runs off the beaters leaves a trail on the surface of the mixture in the bowl for a second or two, you’re there.

STEP 8
Pour the cooled chocolate mixture over the eggy mousse, then gently fold together with a rubber spatula. Plunge the spatula in at one side, take it underneath and bring it up the opposite side and in again at the middle. Continue going under and over in a figure of eight, moving the bowl round after each folding so you can get at it from all sides, until the two mixtures are one and the colour is a mottled dark brown. The idea is to marry them without knocking out the air, so be as gentle and slow as you like.

STEP 9
Hold the sieve over the bowl of eggy chocolate mixture and resift the cocoa and flour mixture, shaking the sieve from side to side, to cover the top evenly.

STEP 10
Gently fold in this powder using the same figure of eight action as before. The mixture will look dry and dusty at first, and a bit unpromising, but if you keep going very gently and patiently, it will end up looking gungy and fudgy. Stop just before you feel you should, as you don’t want to overdo this mixing.

STEP 11
Finally, stir in the white and milk chocolate chunks until they’re dotted throughout.

STEP 12
Pour the mixture into the prepared tin, scraping every bit out of the bowl with the spatula. Gently ease the mixture into the corners of the tin and paddle the spatula from side to side across the top to level it.

STEP 13
Put in the oven and set your timer for 25 mins. When the buzzer goes, open the oven, pull the shelf out a bit and gently shake the tin. If the brownie wobbles in the middle, it’s not quite done, so slide it back in and bake for another 5 minutes until the top has a shiny, papery crust and the sides are just beginning to come away from the tin. Take out of the oven.

STEP 14
Leave the whole thing in the tin until completely cold, then, if you’re using the brownie tin, lift up the protruding rim slightly and slide the uncut brownie out on its base. If you’re using a normal tin, lift out the brownie with the foil. Cut into quarters, then cut each quarter into four squares and finally into triangles.

STEP 15
They’ll keep in an airtight container for a good two weeks and in the freezer for up to a month.

In "Muck," players find themselves stranded on a procedurally generated island, tasked with gathering resources, crafting tools, and building shelters to survive against waves of increasingly difficult enemies. The day-night cycle adds a layer of urgency, as nights bring with them tougher foes that require players to strategically plan their activities during the day. The game’s mechanics are straightforward yet rewarding, with a crafting system that encourages exploration and experimentation.

Speedrunning "Muck" involves mastering the game's mechanics and exploiting the randomness of its world generation. My quick completion time is a testament to the game's potential for high-level play, where knowledge of optimal resource locations, efficient crafting routes, and effective combat strategies are key. The game’s procedural nature means that no two runs are the same, adding a fresh challenge to each attempt and keeping the gameplay experience dynamic and engaging.

"Muck" stands out for its charming, low-poly art style and a soundtrack that perfectly complements the game's whimsical yet challenging atmosphere. Despite its simple graphics, the game is visually appealing, with a bright and colorful palette that makes exploring the island a joy. The combat is straightforward but satisfying, with a variety of weapons and enemies that keep players on their toes.

The game's community has also played a significant role in its success, with players sharing tips, strategies, and custom modifications that add even more depth to the experience. "Muck" encourages both solo and multiplayer gameplay, allowing friends to team up and tackle the island’s challenges together, which adds a layer of cooperative strategy to the mix.

In conclusion, "Muck" is a gem in the survival genre, offering a blend of simplicity and depth that is both accessible and challenging. As a professional speedrunner, completing the game in record time highlights the intricate planning and execution required to master its mechanics. Whether you’re looking to survive for as long as possible, explore a procedurally generated world, or test your skills in a speedrun, "Muck" provides a highly enjoyable and replayable experience. Muck™ quite possibly one of the most riveting and breathtaking games ever made. To play muck all the way through requires dedication and loyalty most of all. Muck's story not only critiques capitalism and the will for survival in a pre-industrial age society but it also challenges colonialism as you as a player are dropped into an unfamiliar world and you are challenged with moral decisions on whether you should improve the lives of these peoples or conquer them for profit. Muck™ is one of the most prolific games of the 21st century and has been genre defining in its category. It outshines many of the triple-A games through its simplicity yet complex and ground breaking story. Muck is not only a game of survival but survival among the fittest. This game is the synthesis of Red Dead Redemption's story, Grand Theft Auto comedic elements, and the grittiness fallout series all packed into a magnificent game. To truly understand Muck is to delve into original philosophy and literature; a prerequisite of playing Muck is to have read Marxist dialectic to truly understand how this game came to be through the decade process of thesis-antithesis-synthesis. All games that have been made before this have served to refine the game to its sharpest point and games made after Muck™ take direct inspiration from this. We see Muck's influence in not only the riveting story of Cyberpunk 2077 but its choreography has directly inspired the Dune movie. Overall this game has been one of the most influential and groundbreaking games that has ever touched human media. To say that this game was influential would be an understatement; Muck should be considered one of the most prolific games with a groundbreaking story.

Excessively long loading times further exacerbate the frustration, breaking the flow of gameplay and testing the player’s patience. TLDR: It's pretty fun...if you have a big group to play it with. I mean BIG.

Imagine the physics-based graphics and humor of TABS/TABG in the form of a survival game. That's Muck. It's fun for fun's sake, and its beautiful simplicity doesn't leave much to be desired.

Don't be fooled by its goofy exterior, though...it's SUPER punishing!
My main problem with the game is that the difficulty of enemies skyrockets each in-game night with no way to balance it except for expensive upgrades and sparse resources. I play with 3 other people, and we barely survive 2-3 days even when working together. I think you'd need 7-10 people to last a week or more.

Another reason to play this with a large group is that each player gets 1 life unless revived, and the host has to start an entirely new server if all the players die. This gets tedious quickly if your friend group is on the small (and, therefore, more-likely-to-die-in-Muck) side.

Contrary to what the devs would have you believe, though, it's not a mistake to try Muck out. For me and my friends, it's worth a good 30-60 minutes of fun every once in a while. I think large community groups would get more out of it, though.

This game will Muck you up!

When my friend KitMcWhiskerton and I orginally played this game, we thought it looked similar to that of Minecraft, but with a Risk of Rain 2 element thrown in as well. Where during the daytime, mobs don't spawn, you're able to gather resources, build a base, and peacefully roam your surroundings. Then during the nighttime that's when an abundance of mobs spawn, and you either hunker down in your base and wait until morning, or you fight for survival and try to gather item drops from slaying creatures. Well, this is all mostly accurate and correct, except that Muck doesn't mess around in the slightest. This game is as chaotic and fast paced as they come! Don't get caught Mucking around, otherwise you're going to get Mucked up!

To begin, you start the game with no items, no abilities and your first task is to try and find a rock so that you can destroy trees, large boulders and hurt mobs more effectively. Since it's the first day in-game, mobs don't pose much of a threat - yet. Some mobs have a percentage chance to drop rare items or abilities which can help your character become more powerful. Upon slaying more mobs you're able to collect points which can be used as a form of currency in this game to open chests, which also hold abilities or items within for you to utilize. As the days progress in-game, the tougher the mobs become... and I don't say that lightly. This is Muck after all... and Muck doesn't mess around.

Apart from your normal mobs that spawn, there is also statues you can interact with that can spawn bosses. Some of these bosses include: Big Chunk, Chief, Guardian and Gronk. Upon defeating a boss they will give you rare items or drops. But let me tell you this... the first time I faced off against Gronk, I was absolutely, unequivocally, indisputably... decimated. Gronk is absolutely disgusting! Do not Muck with Gronk! He is a god amongst men I say! A god! A literal god of terror and death!

Ahem... Anyways... the further you progress in the game, the harder the days become... and some of these bosses that got summoned only by interacting with a statue eventually become a mob that periodically gets summoned depending on what day you are on. This game can get out of hand very quickly and Muck you up. If you thought one Gronk was bad enough... heh, you have no Mucking idea...

The goal of this game is to not only survive for as long as possible, but eventually build components of a large ship and try to escape Muck. To fix up the vessel you have to gather resources from the world and defeat various bosses. Once you have completed building the shipwrecked boat you can set sail and leave Muck. But once you set sail, are you truly safe? Are you free from Muck? No, not yet.

If you have gotten to the point of setting sail with this ship, you encounter the final boss of Muck: Bob.
Bob is a green dragon with luminescent wings and horns. Bob's health surpasses any other boss in the game, and his attacks sure do pack a paralyzing punch. Though Bob drops nothing on defeat, once you have slayed this green dragon, you have completed Muck.

So... what do I think about Muck from playing it and experiencing it all with my dear friend KitMcWhiskerton? Well I do think it is an absolutely beautiful game, both graphically and with its gameplay choices. However, when I retrospectively look back on the memories of running for my Mucking life from Gronk and other various mobs, I don't remember it being, well... the best of times. But with that said, Muck is a gem of a game, and it's the best meme game I have ever played. If you want a difficult game to play, look no further! Muck is here to Muck you up!

I rate Muck as an 8/10 game. If it still received updates and new additions from the creator Dani, I would rate it higher. But as it is,  it hasn't received any new features since 2021. But with that said, it's still a lot of fun, and it's so Mucking difficult!

Do not Guarantee. Not a survival game; more like a game to make you rage quit. I have played survival games over the years and I DO NOT CATEGORIZE THIS AS A SURVIVAL GAME BECAUSE IT LACKS BASIC SURVIVAL GAME MECHANICS. Details below.

If you don't want the details, skip to Overall why this game lacks basic mechanics below.

Breakdown:

GAMEPLAY:
GRAPHICS: 
- Graphics for a free game is okay; however I did experience LAG with other players
- Adjusting and lowering the graphics have little impact to LAG
- There is a FPS counter shown on the top left corner
- For a multiplayer game this part was the worst: Lag occur more with other players. This also caused freeze frames which made it hard during combat

MULTIPLAYER:
- LAG as mention with multiplayer
-All lobby is public; no private gaming
- Copy and Paste LOBBY ID type game to join. No issues with joining.

GAMEPLAY:
- NO SAVE. Once you quit the game, you lose all progress. Once all players die; have to restart with a new game.
- TIME OF DAY: Very short. Does not give enough time as a survival game to gather resources.
- Villagers; Will probably kill you. There is chest with good loot for a beginner to take, but the villager will see and mob you. Villagers has some good trade, however there is only a small list to trade.  

                  MOBS:
- The first wave ON EASY is NOT EASY! There is three to four on the FIRST NIGHT.
- Stronger than your character. HARD TO KILL. More HP and hit damage than character has even with first generation of tools.
- DEFEAT PHYSICS. Unlike character, mobs do not have stamina. THEY CAN ATTACK MELEE AGAINST BASES UNDER WATER AND DO NOT DROWN. RANGE ATTACKS CAN GO THROUGH WALLS, SO WHATS THE POINT OF BUILDING THEM???!!!
- The night wave escalation has NO CHILL. The Build-up between the first three days make it impossible for survival because the mobs are at this point at higher level attack and Hit points.
- CHALLENGES: The mobs are a little stronger than the average mob, but unless you are in creative mode, you will die before you could even attempt them.

POWER-UPS:
- Are too expensive of a price. The chest are purchase with gold obtained from mobs.
- Not enough free chests to give players a actually chance.
- There are a lot of challenges; but there is no point. Challenge mobs are a little stronger than the average mob. However, I was not able to build up enough on weapons, armor or food to try to attempt them. 

OVERALL WHY THIS GAME LACKS BASIC SURVIVAL GAME MECHANICS:
- DEAD GAME: Has not been updated since June 2021.
- Mobs are stronger, invincible, and have less vulnerability than player character AT START. -` - Mobs does not define physics like character.
-NO SAVE
-NO BUILD-UP. There is not way for a player to have build-up of resources or anything because of short time of day and mobs.
-NO POINT IN BASE BUILDS. What is the point of a build if the mob can attack through walls or not die from drowning?
- GUARANTEE DEATH (even on easy mode)
- NO POINT IN STORY. I mean, I couldn't even write a review of the story because I was not able to get pass the third day on EASY with a friend. So.. What is the whole point of making one?
- If you want to enjoy this game; The only way is challenge mode. No mobs at night, but it will be harder to get gold to pay for anything. Also you can build the boat but nothing will happen because the story mode is off.

Title: Muck - An Aimless Adventure

Rating: ★★☆☆☆

Muck is a survival game that promises an exhilarating journey through randomly generated worlds filled with danger and opportunity. However, beneath its flashy exterior lies a game that struggles to find its purpose, leaving players wandering aimlessly in search of meaning.

At first glance, Muck impresses with its colorful graphics and dynamic environments. The freedom to explore, gather resources, and craft items initially sparks excitement, but this enthusiasm quickly fades as players realize the lack of depth in gameplay mechanics. 

One of the most glaring issues with Muck is its lack of direction. While some may appreciate the open-ended nature of the game, others find themselves frustrated by the absence of clear objectives or progression paths. Without a compelling narrative or overarching goal to strive for, gameplay quickly devolves into a repetitive cycle of gathering resources and fending off enemies.

Combat in Muck feels clunky and unrefined, detracting from what could have been a thrilling aspect of the game. The variety of weapons and enemies is limited, resulting in encounters that feel stale and uninspired. Additionally, the absence of meaningful consequences for death undermines the sense of challenge, making encounters with enemies feel more like inconveniences than genuine threats.

Despite its shortcomings, Muck does have its redeeming qualities. The game's multiplayer mode allows for cooperative play, which can enhance the overall experience for those seeking social interaction. Additionally, the game's procedurally generated worlds offer a degree of replayability, though this novelty wears thin after repeated playthroughs.

In conclusion, Muck falls short of its potential, offering a shallow and directionless experience that fails to engage players in a meaningful way. While it may appeal to fans of the survival genre looking for a casual diversion, those seeking depth and purpose in their gaming experiences are likely to be left wanting.

Здравствуйте, все помнят бульдога моего друга по кличке Яйцо? Он рассказывал о нём в обзоре под Lethal Company. Так вот, рассказал бы я про него сразу, но надо бы прежде рассказать про его хозяина, Анатолия Шария. Этот Толя, сын ♥♥♥♥♥, играл во многие игры сегодняшнего мира и, естественно, написал про эти игры обзоры. Короче, ужасный человек. Так, короче. Его псина по кличке Яйцо. В своём детстве этот сучёныш забежал к соседней сучке в будку и жёстко выебал её, за что получил солью из ружья и ослеп. Кстати, я уже говорил, что этой сучке было 18 и да - она была прекрасна. Я бы и сам её трахнул, будь бы шанс. У неё тогда был парень, но она настолько захотела этого пса в моменте, что не устояла перед ним. А вообще, этот тупой псендель не раз меня сейвил. Ща расскажу.. Короче, это было жаркое утро 16-го года. Деревня. Знойный запах коровьего дерьма давал мне просраться. Но это было поистине лучшее время моей жизни. Так вот - иду я по улице, и тут, откуда не возьмись, вылетает копейка с отрядом чурок внутри. А я в этот момент как раз псинку выгуливал за Толю, и сразу встал чтобы не задавили. Но ♥♥♥♥, случилось самое неприятное - эти чуркаши остановились напротив меня. "Закурить есссь, ежжи биля". Жадно пожимая ещё дедовскую пачку Lucky Strike, я ответил: "Нет". Но они явно догадались, что я лукавлю. Повылетали из машины, и начали идти на меня. И тут самое интересное. Яйцо затаил большую обиду на моего дядю, но зная, что его хавать нельзя, копил эту манну на каждый случай. Его единственный глаз работал как прицел. Головка захвата для самонаводящейся ракеты. Так вот. Не успел я сообразить, как этот пёс, в лучших традициях старых мультиков, обежал всех гостей и отхуярил им яйца на корню. Удивительный зверь. Но, как мы знаем, хорошие друзья живут недолго. I am 32 years old.

My ex-wife and I have a daughter together, and we adopted our son together. Both are now 4 years old.

When we were going through our separation, I felt lost and unhappy. I was self-destructive. One day, I was so angry with everything spiraling out of control that I punched a concrete wall in a moment of overwhelming emotion. This resulted in breaking my fifth metacarpal in my right hand—the hand I worked with, played games with, and used to carry my children to bed—the hand I desperately needed to ensure I could continue providing.

Upon learning the severity of the self-inflicted damage, I became almost suicidal. Keep in mind that just a few months before this, I was the happiest man, with no history of depression or anxiety. I had never experienced anger outbursts, nor was I the type to break down and cry, but I was in a tough situation that truly prevented me from seeing the light on the other side.

With nothing better to do, I looked for a game I could play WITH ONE HAND while recovering. Somehow, I stumbled upon this game and read some of the comments. I decided it was worth a try... I must admit I didn't beat the game, nor did I play as much as some of you. In fact, I may have played this game for only a day or two. That being said, after doing so, I had a new joy and hope for life. I managed to leave behind the pain and suffering that had been thrust upon me. I could experience the joy and happiness of other people. I relaxed for 5 ♥♥♥♥ minutes listening to this music, long enough to realize that I would be okay.

After realizing this, I turned off the game and went back to work. My hand hurt a lot, but I was motivated. I stopped feeling so sorry for myself and became the father I needed to be at that moment, not the weak boy I was behaving like.

Today, I am close friends with the mother of my children. We don't fight, argue, or say hurtful things to each other. We are parents and friends.

Now I have 3 children. My third child is, wait, ALSO 4 YEARS OLD. The woman I am with was going through a very similar situation at the time of my separation, and we just unexpectedly stumbled into each other's lives. We have been dating for a year and are very happy together.

Moral of the story: you never know what life has in store for you, and if I had given up when all odds were against me, I wouldn't be where I am today. This silly little game helped me realize that.

Thank you.

Man I really want to love this game. It's a shame it feels like a meme game made for laughs. This game has so much potential, but so much of it feels broken and overly challenging, to the point where it becomes unfair. Not the "fun" unfair, like Getting Over It; but the kind of unfair that just makes you feel sad... really really sad. And that's how I feel about this game, it feels so close to greatness, but when i'm on a really nice streak and just about to unlock steel tools, a bunch of rock golems spawn right behind me and throw a bunch of rocks, dropping my health to 10. Then I start running away, and i sift through my inventory for any shrooms or meat that may bring my health up, only to get bone'd by one of the little human-looking mobs, killing me instantly. Buildings are utterly pointless, as every mob starts ganging up on the nearest structure the first chance they get, and it only takes a few for them to absolutely shred through it. The mobs also don't burn during the day, making daytime just as much of a nuisance, since now you have to clean up all the mobs that spawned at night, but thankfully no new ones spawn while the sun is out. Maybe also add a version of just regular survival, no rogue-like aspect. I know the rogue-like can raise the stakes of the game and bring up tension for some, but to me it just adds to the frustration, especially when you get ganged up on by 6 mobs that just spawned behind you, making your death absolutely no fault of your own. I write this review with tears in my eyes, and an aching in my heart, knowing that these changes will never come, seeing as the developer has abandoned this game completely, the last update was in 2021.

MUCK is a difficult survival game with one encapsulating objective; finding a way to escape the island.


I've had, overall, decent experiences through Multiplayer, minus occasional the desync when a player is slain, drops all of their items, and then cannot find half of those things- even when respawned within mere seconds via a certain statue-- because of those items being invisible to that player.

Some of my frustrations in solo came from the fact that I started on Normal difficulty (selected by default), instead of Easy mode to learn the basics of the game and what-not.


There was a time I tried to access other windows outside of MUCK, and the game locked up- froze, couldn't do or see anything at all-- and I had to close it, losing that run since there's no save functionality that I know of. I later learned to go through the in-game Settings > Video > Fullscreen Mode, and to change it from ExclusiveFullScreen to FullScreenWindow, this also increased overall frame-rate performance that wasn't necessary.


More for story-telling than technical continuations; In a seedless run, I spawned near a cave (honestly looks like a brown igloo), went into it and found at least one node of every single ore in the game right there. 
 Had some trouble getting certain types of equipment due to other material requirements, but was a step below end-game armor on Day 4.
  Mind you, this run was on Easy difficulty to merely get the achievement for completing it.
   I got a claw from one creature, and then a different claw from another- with that second claw, I made a really neat dagger and proceeded to conquer the rest of the island in that run, practically obliterating anything that stood in my way within mere seconds due to the aid of power-ups.
    I finished that run on Day 26, after I was pretty certain there wasn't much left on that island.
      [url=https://steamcommunity.com/id/dragsfeetallday/screenshot/2294085177756980950/]This[/url] is the last screenshot I took of that run.



Solo or with a party, give MUCK a try and see how far you can get!

Some people deem it as too grindy/punishing, and I did see it as that when I first started playing. The key is to focus on collecting as many perks as possible before doing tons of farming. It makes it much more bearable.

A surprising amount of content is in game. Sometimes it gets recycled (some monsters/bosses get a 'skull icon' and a size increase to indicate they're more powerful) but there's enough to keep it refreshing. 

The main negative is that it takes about 2 or 3 hours to beat the game, and there's no way to save, so you have to have 2 or 3 hours of spare time to complete the game set aside. If you're playing solo you can just pause, but with friends it can be a little upsetting if someone has to leave.

There are little to no bugs, at least in my experience. There are some latency issues when people spread out in multiplayer. Sometimes standing on an angled mountain causes the same latency, even in solo play. But that's literally the only bug I've noticed. 

Overall I highly recommend the experience. It took me around 3 or 5 tries to complete the game, each run lasting around 40 minutes to an hour, with the final one being 2 hours long to complete it.

Open world survival, feels Minecraft / Terraria inspired.  Does not seem intended for singleplayer play (no saved progress, not enough time to gather resources before monsters swarm, no way to respawn without the help of another player, etc), and I'm not particularly interested in multiplayer.   General controls seem fine, the scenery's nice, had no graphical or interface problems.

A lot of resources are gated behind needing appropriate tools, so if it looks like your attempt to gather something isn't working, move on to a different resource until you can get a new tool.  This includes all but one kind of tree, and all rocks/ores large enough to see over tall grass.

[DEC 2024 update] : The interface is improved, it's easier to tell when something isn't working, there's more tutorialization, creative mode is very playable as a single player, but there's still no way to save your progress across game sessions.  The lack of ability to save makes it fundamentally fail as both a work-to-unlock-things based game or a crafting/building based game, but if you're the sort of person who sits down to play minecraft, kills the enderdragon same-session, and then never returns to that world again, it might work for you.

I want to start by saying that none of this is sarcasm. While many other reviewers make jokey reviews, I want to focus more seriously on the game itself. Muck is a good game. Heck it might even be a great game. I am not someone to say something like this lightly, if anything I tend to be a more critical person when it comes to games. However Muck is a game that, even if the developer might deny it, has a lot of visible passion put into it. 

Muck is a roguelike, which means this is a trial and error game at its core. You would be forgiven if you looked at this game and weren't immediately impressed but there is a lot of thought that has gone into this. From the mechanics, to the scope, to even just the way that Muck paces itself. You start with nothing and are told to pick up a rock. You use the rock to cut down a tree, you use the wood to make tools, and you use tools to mine and break harder trees. This cycle is continued in much the same way as minecraft where the weapons/armor/tools are in tiers and each tier can mine the next. This game also has a build mechanic, Yes! You can build defensive walls and structures to keep you alive. The enemies are genuinely threatening if not handled correctly and grow stronger as you go along. Food is a precious commodity as it is the only means to fill up your hunger bar and as a result help fill up your stamina. Once your hunger is down, you get no more stamina, and that is a death sentence. 

Muck works in a day to night cycle where every day you are gathering, hunting, and taking on challenges. Then nights where you might hold up in a building trying not to get one shot by a boss or an elite golem. Enemies you defeat drop loot, most commonly of which is gold, you use gold to open chests around the map that give you bonuses for the rest of the play session. There is a really intriguing balance with gold and chests because there are different tiers of chests that require different amounts of gold. So there is always a back and forth in my mind as to whether I save up gold and get a really good bonus or disperse the gold quicker into lower tier chests for quicker low tier bonuses. You might see that I have just 2.9 hours at this point. That isn't a lot admittedly but this game has done something that few other games have. It's made me want to play more, and not just play more but get better, find better strategies, complete the hard achievements on Steam. If you know me personally you would know that once I want to get better at a game then I'm hooked. I haven't experienced the whole game yet and that just makes it more tantalizing for me. I genuinely want to know what the game looks like the further you get. And guess what, it's free! And not that type of free where you start playing and the game then not so subtly shows you the item shop, no it is completely free at least right now. And on top of all that! You can play with your friends and from what I've played with friends the servers are good. 

The biggest issue with the game in my opinion is that enemies, like the goblins can hit you through walls. And not just from AoE attacks, it would seem that if a goblin can get close enough to the wall it can do it's ranged attack and spawn the projectile on the other side of the wall which is frustrating considering that that defeats the purpose of building in the first place, at least from them. 

All in all, Muck is very much worth playing. You may die and get frustrated but there will be no weight missing from your wallet. This is a legitimately good game and I hope that it only gets better.

1/4 tsp. ground allspice

Directions
1
For the pie: Preheat the oven to 400˚F. On a lightly floured surface, roll 1 ball of pie dough into a 13-inch circle. Transfer the crust to a 9-inch pie plate. Tuck the edges of the crust under to be even with the edge of the pie plate and crimp as desired. Place the crust in the refrigerator for 1 hour (or freezer for 30 minutes).
2
Line the inside of the chilled crust with parchment paper, then fill with baking weights or dried beans. Bake until the edges of the crust are very lightly golden, 18 to 22 minutes. Remove the pie weights and parchment paper. Return the crust to the oven and bake until the whole crust is lightly golden all over, 10 to 12 minutes longer. Let cool to room temperature. Reduce the oven to 350˚F.
3
Prick the sweet potatoes all over with a fork and place on a microwave-safe paper towel-lined plate. Microwave on high for 5 minutes and flip. Microwave until the potatoes are tender, about 5 minutes more. Allow to cool for 10 minutes and carefully cut in half lengthwise. When potatoes are cool enough to handle, use a spoon to scoop the flesh into the work bowl of a food processor.
4
Add the butter to the potatoes and pulse the mixture until pureed, scraping down the sides of the bowl. Add the milk, eggs, egg yolks, bourbon, if using, and vanilla. Process until smooth. Add the dark brown sugar, granulated sugar, cinnamon, ginger, nutmeg, allspice, and salt; process until smooth. Pour the filling into the partially baked crust. Bake until the filling is set on the edges but slightly jiggly in the middle, 45 to 55 minutes. Allow to cool completely on a wire rack, 2 hours.
5
For the bourbon whipped cream: In the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the whisk attachment, combine the heavy cream, confectioner's sugar, 1 to 2 tablespoons of bourbon (to taste), and vanilla. Beat on medium-high speed until stiff peaks form, 2 to 4 minutes. Cover and refrigerate until ready to use.
6
Slice the pie and serve with bourbon whipped cream. Cover and refrigerate any remaining pie.

Grass is a type of plant with narrow leaves growing from the base. Their appearance as a common plant was in the mid-Cretaceous period. There are 12,000 species now.[3]

A common kind of grass is used to cover the ground in places such as lawns and parks. Grass is usually the color green. That is because they are wind-pollinated rather than insect-pollinated, so they do not have to attract insects. Green is the best colour for photosynthesis.

Grasslands such as savannah and prairie where grasses are dominant cover 40.5% of the land area of the Earth, except Greenland and Antarctica.[4]

Grasses are monocotyledon herbaceous plants. They include the "grass" of the family Poaceae, which are called grass by ordinary people. This family is also called the Gramineae, and includes some of the sedges (Cyperaceae) and the rushes (Juncaceae).[5] These three families are not very closely related, though all of them belong to clades in the order Poales. They are similar adaptations to a similar life-style.

With about 780 genera and about 12,000 species,[3] the Poaceae is the fifth-largest plant family. Only the Asteraceae, Orchidaceae, Fabaceae and Rubiaceae have more species.[6]

The true grasses include cereals, bamboo and the grasses of lawns (turf) and grassland. Uses for graminoids include food (as grain, shoots or rhizomes), drink (beer, whisky), pasture for livestock, thatch, paper, fuel, clothing, insulation, construction, sports turf, basket weaving and many others.

Many grasses are short, but some grasses can grow tall, such as bamboo. Plants from the grass family can grow in many places and make grasslands, including areas which are very arid or cold. There are several other plants that look similar to grass and are referred to as such, but are not members of the grass family. These plants include rushes, reeds, papyrus and water chestnut. Seagrass is a monocot in the order Alismatales.

Grasses are an important food for many animals, such as deer, buffalo, cattle, mice, grasshoppers, caterpillars and many other grazers. Unlike other plants, grasses grow from the bottom, so when animals eat grass they usually do not destroy the part that grows.[7] This is a part of why the plants are successful. Without grass, soil may wash away into rivers (erosion).

Evolution of grass
Grasses include some of the most versatile plant life-forms. They became widespread toward the end of the Cretaceous. Fossilized dinosaur dung (coprolites) have been found containing grass phytoliths (silica stones inside grass leaves).[8] Grasses have adapted to conditions in lush rain forests, dry deserts, cold mountains and even intertidal habitats, and are now the most widespread plant type. Grass is a valuable source of food and energy for many animals.[9]

Grass and people
Lawn grass is often planted on sports fields and in the area around a building. Sometimes chemicals and water is used to help lawns to grow.

People have used grasses for a long time. People eat parts of grasses. Corn, wheat, barley, oats, rice and millet are cereals, common grains whose seeds are used for food and to make alcohol such as beer.

Sugar comes from sugar cane, which is also a plant in the grass family. People have grown grasses as food for farm animals for about 4,000 years. People use bamboo to build houses, fences, furniture and other things. Grass plants can also be used as fuel, to cover rooves, and to weave baskets.

Language
In English, the word "grass" appears in several phrases. For example:

"The grass is always greener on the other side" means "people are never happy with what they have and want something else".
"Don't let the grass grow under your feet" means "Do something".
"A snake in the grass" is about a person that will not be honest and will trick others.
All flesh is grass: Old Testament book of Isaiah, chapter 40, verses 6–8. A very true observation of the present-day ecology. See the Miocene for the ecological relevance.
Grass is a slang term for cannabis (pot, weed, or marijuana). Cannabis looks like a grass, but it is actually a rosid.

At first this game can be quite hard, but in a fun way. Yet the further you progress the easier it gets. Which of course is great and the purpose of learning from your previous mistakes.
However by that its very easy to get the best gear quite early and then the game looses its challenge and you could get bored quite fast.
Building something isnt really fun cause either you get absolutely obliderated by mosters if you dont focus on your defense first, or they just destroy whatever you have built.
Once you got the hang of it and got your best gear there really isnt any reason to keep playing it as the monsters and bosses that were challenging and fun before now just are a necessary burden that forcefully distract you from your previous goal.

I tried the 100 days achievement with a friend of mine once, which requires you to stay alive 100 days in one game. after about 13 days we had the best equipment, after about 20 days we looted every chest, after about 24 days we mastered every challenge (fought all statues that are available) and then we were bored. We started to destroy every house, tree, ore, rock - whatever we were able to find, built a decent yet awful looking house (as building options are quite limited as the focus of this game isnt building), we towered ourself up and watched youtube videos for 40 more days which took waaaay too long until we finally managed to end the game and got the achievement.

My point here is that you arent rewarded for actually learning the mechanics of the game, but by doing absolutely absurd things nobody would ever like to do, not because they are too hard but because they take insanely long - like the achievement type for "killing 1.000.000 of every type of enemy" that you may know from other games.
To that point the game isnt fun anymore. it drags itself.
And as soon you started to understand the game mechanic there, first, isnt a reason to do anything different to what you did before, and second, you notice that its almost impossible to change your tactics as you have to level up as fast as your enemies do, otherwise you are doomed.
Means: you gotta level up first to almost the maximum as fast as possible, and then you are free to do whatever you like to do, but because the game isnt designed to do much different other than fighting these other activities get boring quite fast.

I like the bosses, they are all very challenging and fun to beat, except Chief maybe, cause he is just unfairly fast sometimes, and the laser of the guardian can be quite unfair sometimes as well. But otherwise they were quite fun, simple yet nicely designed and really rewarding when you beat them.
However, if you fought the same boss 30 times in a row now it sure starts to get boring.

With more variety in the fights, with more exploring and a slower start to the action this game could have been a lot of fun, though this way its just really annoyingly boring. 3/10

"Muck." What a weird name for a game. I don't know what to think. But much like it's weird name, it is weirdly fun. For a free game, its quite good! Lots to do and explore, and plays kind of similarly to Minecraft. But...

Its hard as balls, and you will lose A LOT. That is part of the appeal, as it can be fun to trial and error against an unknown world. But just know what you're getting into. Combat is brutal, and until you get a decent weapon every night is a fight for your life. Even after, bossfights will still kick your ass into the sun. Yes, there are bossfights, by the way. There wasn't really any way i found that you could save, and lobbying for multiplayer is clunky and could use some streamlining. So it is not an experience without frustration... 

That all said, it is a damn good free game that will probably provide hours of content if you choose to pursue it. In fact i think i like it way more than Minecraft. All Achievements run of Muck, anyone?

Muck, a delightful and comically engaging game, proves to be a rollercoaster of entertainment with a unique blend of challenge and humor. Developed by a small indie team, this title is a testament to their creative prowess and dedication to creating an unforgettable gaming experience. While Muck offers a genuinely fun and humorous ride, it's worth noting that its level of difficulty might leave some players scratching their heads.

At first glance, Muck's quirky art style and endearing character design set the tone for an unconventional journey. The game's lighthearted approach to survival mechanics and resource gathering immediately puts a smile on your face. The sandbox environment encourages exploration, creativity, and experimentation. From crafting outrageously imaginative weapons to building your dream shelter, every step in Muck feels like a chance to flex your imaginative muscles.

However, it doesn't take long for Muck to reveal its true colors in terms of difficulty. The game has a tendency to throw curveballs at players, challenging them to think on their feet and adapt to the ever-changing landscape. The randomly generated world, while keeping gameplay fresh, can also present unexpected hurdles that demand quick thinking and well-laid plans. This aspect, while thrilling for those seeking a true test of their skills, might prove frustrating for players who prefer a more laid-back experience.

The multiplayer option in Muck adds another layer of excitement to the mix. Collaborating with friends to overcome the game's challenges can lead to hilarious mishaps and triumphs alike. The camaraderie forged in the face of adversity is where Muck shines brightest, turning difficulty into an opportunity for bonding and shared laughter.

In summary, Muck is an absolute gem of a game, combining humor, creativity, and survival mechanics in a way that's as entertaining as it is unpredictable. Its unique blend of challenge and charm keeps players engaged and eager to explore its vibrant world. However, the game's difficulty might be a stumbling block for some, requiring a level of perseverance that not all players might possess. If you're up for a good laugh and don't mind some hair-pulling moments of frustration, Muck is definitely worth a shot. Just be prepared to embrace the chaos and savor the victories that come from conquering its challenges.

Title: Muck - A Challenging Survival Adventure in an Ever-Changing World

Rating: ★★★★☆ (4/5)

Review:

Muck is an ambitious early access survival game that plunges players into a procedurally generated world filled with challenges and dangers. Developed by a solo developer, the game has garnered attention for its sandbox-style gameplay and relentless difficulty, offering a thrilling experience for fans of survival and exploration.

The game's minimalist graphics and blocky art style add a nostalgic charm that harks back to classic voxel-based games. While the visuals might be modest, Muck's dynamic world and adaptive mechanics more than compensate for its simplistic appearance.

At its core, Muck is about surviving the elements, gathering resources, and fending off hordes of hostile creatures that lurk in the dark. Players start with nothing more than their wits and must quickly learn to adapt to their surroundings, constructing shelters, crafting tools, and hunting for food.

The real challenge of Muck lies in its unforgiving difficulty. The game becomes progressively harder with each passing day, as powerful enemies and tougher biomes test players' ability to strategize and survive. The ever-increasing intensity provides a sense of accomplishment for those who manage to stay alive.

Muck encourages player creativity through its crafting system, which allows for a variety of weapon and tool combinations. As players gather resources, they can craft better equipment to tackle more formidable foes, leading to a satisfying sense of progression.

One of the game's standout features is its multiplayer functionality, where players can team up with friends to tackle the harsh world together. Cooperation and communication are key in overcoming Muck's challenges, making the multiplayer experience particularly enjoyable.

However, being in early access, Muck is not without its drawbacks. Some players have reported encountering bugs and issues that can occasionally hinder gameplay. Additionally, the game's limited content and lack of end-game goals might leave some players yearning for more once they have mastered the survival aspect.

In conclusion, Muck is a promising survival game with an intriguing concept and challenging gameplay. Its dynamic world and multiplayer capabilities provide hours of entertainment, and its replay value stems from the unpredictable nature of the procedurally generated environment. While some aspects may require refinement, Muck is an early access gem worth exploring for fans of survival and adventure games.

How to make homemade milk

If your looking for a actually review this isnt the one.

-----------------------------------
You will need:
-a cow
-vacuum cups
-stainless steel pipes
-large refrigerated vats
-tankers
-fine nozzles
-Centrifugal separation
-Ultrafiltration
-Reverse osmosis
-Ultra osmosis
-Spray drying
-----------------------------------
STEP ONE:
-----------------------------------
Milk the cows teats by attaching vacuum cups, after your done with that sent the milk thorugh stainless steel pipes to large refrigerated vats then store is for 5°C or less. Within 48 hours (or 2 days) move the milk in tankers to your home or any building with necesary supplies.
-----------------------------------
STEP TWO:
-----------------------------------
You will need to pasteurisatite the milk. Pasteurisation is a technique that heats the milk to 72°C for no less than 15 seconds, then cool the milk immediately to destroy any harmful bacteria and micro-organisms and also to extend the milks shelf life.
-----------------------------------
STEP THREE
-----------------------------------
Put the milk under pressure through fine nozzles, which evenly disperses fat globules. This stops the cream separating and rising to the top, allowing a more consistent texture and taste.
-----------------------------------
STEP FOUR:
-----------------------------------
Centrifugaly separatite the milk. Centrifugal separation removes some or all of the cream to make reduced-fat, low-fat or skim milk. Skim milk solids can be added back to improve the test and texture, and increase nutrients like protein and calcium. 
-----------------------------------
STEP FIVE:
-----------------------------------
Ultrafiltratite the milk. Ultrafiltration moves milk across a membrane under  moderate pressure, which holds back protein, fat globules, and a large amount of calcium complexes, water and lactose (the sugar in milk) pass through, leaving behind a very protein and calcium-rich product. The fat content can be adjusted to suit consumer preference.
-----------------------------------
STEP SIX:
-----------------------------------
Reverse osmosis the milk. Reverse osmosis is very similar to ultrafiltration, but the membrane holds back most of the milk solids and only lets water pass through. Lactose remains in the product, so there is no impact on flavour.
-----------------------------------
STEP SEVEN:
-----------------------------------
Ultra osmosis the milk. Ultra osmosis is a combination of ultrafiltration and reverse osmosis, but it holds back milk solids and allows both water and salt to pass through.
-----------------------------------
STEP EIGHT:
-----------------------------------
Serve and enjoy!
-----------------------------------

If you are looking for a review on Brawlhalla you have come to the wrong place but, I can tell you how to make delicious Butter Chicken.
-----------------------------------------------------------
Ingredients for 4 servings,
2 lb boneless, skinless chicken breast (910 g), cubed
salt, to taste
pepper, to taste
2 teaspoons chili powder, divided
½ teaspoon turmeric
6 tablespoons butter, divided
1 ½ cups yellow onion (225 g), diced
3 teaspoons garam masala
1 teaspoon cumin
1 teaspoon cayenne pepper
1 tablespoon ginger, grated
3 cloves garlic, minced
1 cinnamon, 3 inch (8 cm) stick
14 oz tomato sauce (395 g)
1 cup water (240 mL)
1 cup heavy cream (240 mL)
rice, for serving
fresh cilantro, chopped for garnish.

Preparation
In a large bowl, season the chicken breast with salt, pepper, 1 teaspoon of chili powder, and the teaspoon of turmeric. Let
sit for 15 minutes to marinate.
Melt 2 tablespoons of butter in a large pot over medium heat. Brown the chicken, then remove from the pot.
Melt another 2 tablespoons of butter in the pot, then add the onion, garam masala, remaining teaspoon of chili powder,
the cumin, ginger, garlic, cayenne, cinnamon, salt and pepper. Cook until fragrant.
Add the tomato sauce and bring to a simmer.
Add the water and cream and return to a simmer.
Return the chicken to the pot, cover, and simmer for another 10-15 minutes.
Stir in the last 2 tablespoons of butter and season with more salt and pepper to taste.
Serve the chicken over rice and garnish with cilantro.
Enjoy!

Muck is a masterpiece, having mastered the art of showing without telling. As a result, it is very different from other open-world games I have played such as Skyrim and Far Cry which are story and questline driven. From the get-go, Muck doesn't impose any particular playstyle or route on you. You are completely free to do what you want to from the very start of the game. You can finish the main storyline and beat the final boss or you can explore the entire map without ever seeing the main bosses, it truly is up to you with no outside influence. It is truly refreshing to feel this sense of freedom in choice and exploration in any open world game.

Muck has also mastered the art of sublety. For example, for a game like Skyrim, there are various elements such as the character dialogues, leveling system, various landmarks that I could clearly point to in contributing to the game's success. However, this is not the same with Muck. It's hard to place my finger on one specific thing that makes the game so enjoyable. Many times I've gone in to play this game for half an hour, only to become immersed, losing track of time and playing for hours on end. I belive that it's each of the game's features: its combat system, transportation, landscape, lore, storytelling, etc. that complement each other in a way that none of them are overbearing and at the same time, come together in such a fluid manner that I as the player can't notice it and am drawn into a level of immersion that I haven't felt from any game before.

Other, more objective factors of Muck are equally as impressive--it's hard to believe this isn't a $60 game. The map is massive, far bigger than I could've ever imagined, with more content packed into it than any other world game I've played before. I have not had a single moment where I've felt the map felt desolate or empty, there was always something to see and explore. The combat system is rich, balanced, and rewards each playstyle. The difficulty of the game is refreshing and I feel that I'm being challenged to improve and innovate as I play the game instead of relying on old hacks. The subtle details, such as changes in behavior over time of day or cross-NPC interactions add a layer of immersion that makes the world feel alive. It is also a very polished product: while games today are released with game-breaking bugs and issues, I haven't encountered a single bug in Muck even given its massive map aside from minor visual glitches. It is truly astounding how much that adds to the immersion of the game.

Overall, I feel that Muck is an amazing game. While it isn't perfect by any means, in fact, the imperfections of the game give me something to look forward to for what will be the sequel to this, it will be hard to find a game from the last decade that is as immersive as this. I am truly impressed by Dani work and I look forward to their next game. Muck will inspire the next generation's set of games and I hope to see what comes from this. I've thoroughly enjoyed playing Muck and I hope to see you too enjoy it.

The fun:

Muck is a fun game, its like Minecraft but with the permadeath system in place. Muck allows you to harvest, fight mobs that spawn during the day and night circles. The combat is fairly good, just swing any object at your enemy and watch their health bar slowly deplete. Weather it be a rock, tree log or sword, (Haven't tried the work bench.) 

You get coins from Mobs, which then enables you to open chest. These Chest contains perks, that help your ability, to beat the game quicker. And some are quite fun. What's also nice is the perks stack, so that's nice. 
When I played it, I played it on Easy difficulty. Don't let it fool you, its still quite hard, but less brutal than normal difficulty. There's several different bosses you fight, and six you have to fight to complete one of the steps of the game. (I don't want to spoil).

Now the less fun.

Perhaps the least fun mechanic of the game is the inability to return to a save. Sure, its meant for a very quick play, but in my progress of playing it took me a total four hours to beat Easy. The last two hours of it, I wanted to play something else, but couldn't leave. Sure, I could've left my PC running, but pc's tend to crash, and I didn't want to leave a game that I wasn't really playing on my PC idling. Overall, the game is a 7/10 for me. Do give it a shot, its totally fun with friends, the memories you experience will be full of laughter.

Muck, the phenomenal survival game on Steam, has captivated my gaming senses like no other. From the moment I plunged into its beautifully crafted world, I was immersed in an adventure that pushed my limits and challenged my survival skills. The game's stunning visuals, gripping gameplay mechanics, and dynamic environment combine to deliver an unforgettable experience that keeps me coming back for more.

One of the standout features of Muck is its procedural generation, which ensures that each playthrough is a unique and unpredictable experience. The vast open world is teeming with dangerous creatures, valuable resources, and hidden treasures, begging to be explored. Whether I was venturing into dark caves or scaling towering mountains, the sense of discovery and anticipation never waned, keeping me on the edge of my seat throughout my journey.

Muck offers a wide range of gameplay options that cater to different playstyles. As a survival enthusiast, I thoroughly enjoyed gathering resources, constructing shelters, and crafting powerful weapons to fend off the game's relentless enemies. The skill progression system provided a sense of accomplishment as I honed my abilities and became a formidable force in this harsh world. The game strikes a perfect balance between challenge and reward, making each triumph feel hard-earned and satisfying.

The cooperative multiplayer mode in Muck deserves special mention. Joining forces with friends to survive against hordes of enemies added an exciting layer of teamwork and coordination to the game. Collaborating on base-building, strategizing combat tactics, and sharing resources created a sense of camaraderie that elevated the experience to new heights. Muck truly shines when played with others, fostering unforgettable moments of triumph and bonding.

The developers of Muck have shown remarkable dedication to their player community. Regular updates and additions ensure that the game stays fresh and engaging. From new biomes and enemies to weapons and items, the evolving content keeps players engaged and excited for what lies ahead. The commitment to addressing player feedback and implementing meaningful changes showcases the developers' passion for creating a thriving and ever-evolving gaming experience.

Muck is a true gem in the survival genre, offering a captivating and exhilarating adventure for gamers seeking a challenging experience. With its visually stunning world, diverse gameplay mechanics, and cooperative multiplayer mode, it exceeds expectations at every turn. Whether you're a fan of survival games or simply looking for an immersive and thrilling gaming experience, Muck is an absolute must-play. Prepare to be hooked from the moment you step foot in this dynamic and unforgiving world.

Muck is a masterpiece, having mastered the art of showing without telling.  As a result, it is very different from other open-world games I have played such as Skyrim and Far Cry which are story and questline driven. From the get-go, Muck doesn't impose any particular playstyle or route on you. You are completely free to do what you want to from the very start of the game. You can finish the main storyline and beat the final boss or you can explore the entire map without ever seeing the main bosses, it truly is up to you with no outside influence. It is truly refreshing to feel this sense of freedom in choice and exploration in any open world game.

Muck has also mastered the art of sublety. For example, for a game like Skyrim, there are various elements such as the character dialogues, leveling system, various landmarks that I could clearly point to in contributing to the game's success. However, this is not the same with Muck. It's hard to place my finger on one specific thing that makes the game so enjoyable. Many times I've gone in to play this game for half an hour, only to become immersed, losing track of time and playing for hours on end. I belive that it's each of the game's features: its combat system, transportation, landscape, lore, storytelling, etc. that complement each other in a way that none of them are overbearing and at the same time, come together in such a fluid manner that I as the player can't notice it and am drawn into a level of immersion that I haven't felt from any game before.

Other, more objective factors of Muck are equally as impressive--it's hard to believe this is a $60 game. The map is massive, far bigger than I could've ever imagined, with more content packed into it than any other world game I've played before. I have not had a single moment where I've felt the map felt desolate or empty, there was always something to see and explore. The combat system is rich, balanced, and rewards each playstyle. The difficulty of the game is refreshing and I feel that I'm being challenged to improve and innovate as I play the game instead of relying on old hacks. The subtle details, such as changes in behavior over time of day or cross-NPC interactions add a layer of immersion that makes the world feel alive. It is also a very polished product: while games today are released with game-breaking bugs and issues, I haven't encountered a single bug in Muck even given its massive map aside from minor visual glitches. It is truly astounding how much that adds to the immersion of the game.

Overall, I feel that Muck is an amazing game. While it isn't perfect by any means, in fact, the imperfections of the game give me something to look forward to for what will be the sequel to this, it will be hard to find a game from the last decade that is as immersive as this. I am truly impressed by Dani work and I look forward to their next game. Muck will inspire the next generation's set of games and I hope to see what comes from this. I've thoroughly enjoyed playing Muck and I hope to see you too enjoy it.

One of the most thrilling experiences in gaming is overcoming a challenging obstacle. That feeling of satisfaction after struggling through a tough section of gameplay is unbeatable. If you're looking for a game that will give you that sense of accomplishment, look no further than Muck.

Muck is without a doubt the best video game i have played in years. The game throws you into a procedurally generated world filled with hostile creatures, limited resources, and harsh environmental conditions. You'll need to gather resources, craft weapons and armor, build shelters, and fight off waves of enemies to survive. However, the enemies are relentless and powerful, and death can come swiftly if you're not careful. The game punishes mistakes, and you'll likely die multiple times before mastering its mechanics and strategies. Despite its difficulty, Muck remains incredibly fun to play. The sense of accomplishment and satisfaction that comes from overcoming challenges and surviving against all odds is immensely rewarding. Each time you learn from your mistakes, adapt your strategies, and make progress, you'll feel a surge of excitement and accomplishment. The feeling of achievement when you finally defeat a powerful enemy or find a rare resource is unparalleled, and it keeps you coming back for more, even after countless failures. Muck will have your balls quaking while you play it. Every time you die you'll be on your knees begging for more.

All in all, Muck is certainly the best game published in the past 10 years, perhaps ever. I've developed an addiction to CBT after the amount of times I crushed my penis with a rock playing this game. Despite this, I highly recommend this game to anyone that finds it on the steam workshop.
